credit.bank_branches.plain: How many offices of FDIC-insured banks each municipio has, every June 30.
credit.bank_branches.plain_es: Cuántas oficinas de bancos asegurados por la FDIC tiene cada municipio, cada 30 de junio.
credit.bank_branches.definition: The offices of FDIC-insured banks in the municipio on June 30: main offices, branches and limited-service offices, as the banks report them to the FDIC each year. Cooperativas de ahorro y crédito are insured by COSSEC, not the FDIC, and are not counted: a municipio with no bank office may still have a cooperativa.
credit.bank_branches.method: credit.py reads every office of an FDIC-insured bank in Puerto Rico in the Summary of Deposits, June 30 of each year 2000-2026, and adds them up by the municipio the FDIC gives each office (STCNTYBR). The FDIC's survey covers main offices, branches and limited-service offices of every insured bank; deposits are in thousands of dollars in the file and in dollars here.
credit.bank_branches.how_to_read: Puerto Rico had 571 bank offices in 2006 and 260 in 2026. Most lost since 2006: San Juan (68), Carolina (24), Ponce (22), Bayamón (21). No FDIC-insured office in 2026: Cataño, Guánica. Per 1,000 residents, the Analysis tab offers the rate.
caveats: Cooperativas de ahorro y crédito are insured by COSSEC, not the FDIC, and are not counted: a municipio with no bank office may still have a cooperativa.
An office counts the same whether it is a full branch or a limited-service office inside a store.
The FDIC places about half the offices at the centre of their ZIP code since 2023 (113 of 260 have a street-level location in 2026), so the observatory draws no office points.
credit.bank_branches.source_detail: FDIC Summary of Deposits, June 30 of each year, 2000-2026

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (group Economy · Banks and deposits (FDIC)): Bank offices (FDIC-insured banks)

credit.bank_deposits.plain: How much money FDIC-insured banks hold in deposits at their offices in each municipio, every June 30.
credit.bank_deposits.plain_es: Cuánto dinero en depósitos tienen los bancos asegurados por la FDIC en sus oficinas de cada municipio, cada 30 de junio.
credit.bank_deposits.definition: The deposits that FDIC-insured banks book at their offices in the municipio on June 30, in dollars of each year (not adjusted for inflation). Deposits are counted where the bank books them, not where the depositors live: a bank's main office books far more than its share, so San Juan holds most of the island's total. Cooperativas de ahorro y crédito are insured by COSSEC, not the FDIC, and are not counted: a municipio with no bank office may still have a cooperativa.
credit.bank_deposits.method: credit.py reads every office of an FDIC-insured bank in Puerto Rico in the Summary of Deposits, June 30 of each year 2000-2026, and adds them up by the municipio the FDIC gives each office (STCNTYBR). The FDIC's survey covers main offices, branches and limited-service offices of every insured bank; deposits are in thousands of dollars in the file and in dollars here.
credit.bank_deposits.how_to_read: Puerto Rico: $85.54 billion in 2026 ($30.35 billion in 2000). Most: San Juan ($56.22 billion), Bayamón ($3.32 billion), Guaynabo ($2.82 billion).
caveats: Deposits are counted where the bank books them, not where the depositors live: a main office books far more than its share, so San Juan holds most of the island's total.
Dollars of each year, not adjusted for inflation.
Cooperativas de ahorro y crédito are insured by COSSEC, not the FDIC, and are not counted: a municipio with no bank office may still have a cooperativa.
credit.bank_deposits.source_detail: FDIC Summary of Deposits, June 30 of each year, 2000-2026

municipalities.income_change_pct.plain: How much the median household income changed between the 2008-2012 survey window and the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), in percent. Each window is in the dollars of its own last year (2012 and 2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot), so general price rises are still in the number.
municipalities.income_change_pct.plain_es: Cuánto cambió el ingreso mediano de los hogares entre la ventana de encuesta 2008-2012 y la más reciente (2020-2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10), en por ciento. Cada ventana está en dólares de su propio último año (2012 y 2024 en el corte de datos de 2026-10), así que el alza general de precios sigue incluida en el número.
municipalities.income_change_pct.definition: (median_hh_income in the latest window minus median_hh_income in the 2008-2012 window) divided by the 2008-2012 value, times 100. The latest window is 2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot. Both medians are table B19013 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates. The Census Bureau reports ACS dollar amounts in the dollars of the last year of each window, and the 2008-2012 table is titled 'in 2012 inflation-adjusted dollars'. So the 2008-2012 window is in 2012 dollars and the latest window is in the dollars of its last year (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The observatory makes no conversion between windows.
municipalities.income_change_pct.method: Calculated as round((new − old) ÷ old × 100, 1), where new is B19013 cell 001 for the latest window and old is the same cell for 2008-2012. The field is empty if the old value is missing or zero.
municipalities.income_change_pct.how_to_read: A positive value means the median household has more dollars of income than in 2008-2012. In the 2026-10 snapshot, every municipality shows more dollars of income than in 2008-2012, but 34 of 78 rose by less than the 36.6% rise in the US CPI-U over 2012 to 2024. A rise in dollars is not a rise in buying power. On the Housing page you can choose another base year, and the page then shows a different comparison. This field always compares 2008-2012 with the latest window. To cite it in the 2026-10 snapshot, write 'ACS 5-year estimates, 2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012, table B19013, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory'.
caveats: The observatory does not convert 2012 dollars to 2024 dollars, so the change includes general price rises. For scale, the US Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) rose 36.6% from 2012 to 2024 (annual averages, stored in economy_series.json). The CPI-U is a US index of all consumer prices. It is not a Puerto Rico index and not a measure of rent or home-price inflation, so it is only a rough scale.

Both ends are survey estimates with their own margins of error. A small change in a small municipality can be noise. The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.

nightlights.ntl_radiance.plain: How bright the area is at night, as NASA's satellite sees it: the average light of the area's pixels over the year. Brighter usually means more activity and power; a sudden drop can mean a blackout.
nightlights.ntl_radiance.plain_es: Cuán brillante es el área de noche, según el satélite de la NASA: la luz promedio de los píxeles del área durante el año. Más brillo suele significar más actividad y electricidad; una caída repentina puede ser un apagón.
nightlights.ntl_radiance.definition: The mean of the VNP46A3 monthly radiance (AllAngle_Composite_Snow_Free, nW/cm²/sr) of the 15 arc-second pixels whose centre lies in the area, pooled over the twelve months of the calendar year. A municipio's and Puerto Rico's means are over all their pixels.
nightlights.ntl_radiance.method: nightlights.py (methods.nightlights): each monthly HDF5 file of tile h11v07 is read with h5py, each pixel goes to the barrio holding its centre, and the year's mean pools the twelve months' pixels with a value.
nightlights.ntl_radiance.how_to_read: Puerto Rico in 2025: 5.431 nW/cm²/sr. Brightest municipios: San Juan (47.2), Cataño (38.4), Guaynabo (26.2); darkest: Maricao (0.5), Vieques (0.7), Las Marías (0.8). Puerto Rico fell from 5.245 in 2016 to 4.233 in 2017, the year of Hurricane María.
caveats: Clouds: Puerto Rico is often cloudy, mostly from May to November. A month with few clear nights is flagged poor (three or fewer) or gap-filled (none), and its value can lag the real light.

Moonlight: the product removes moonlight with a model (the lunar BRDF correction), so bright-moon and dark-moon months can be compared; the correction has its own error, largest where the light is dim.
Light is a proxy for activity and for electric power, not a count of people, jobs or homes with power. A change can also come from new LED streetlights, whose whiter light the sensor sees less of.
Pixels are about 460 m across and light spills over borders, so a small or dark barrio next to a bright one reads brighter than it is.
nightlights.ntl_radiance.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios
nightlights.ntl_radiance.source_detail: NASA Black Marble VNP46A3 collection 2, https://doi.org/10.5067/VIIRS/VNP46A3.002; Román et al. (2018), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2018.03.017.

nightlights.ntl_poor_pct.plain: How much of the area's night-time light figure rests on few clear nights: the share of its pixels that NASA flags as poor quality or filled in from earlier data, mostly because of clouds.
nightlights.ntl_poor_pct.plain_es: Cuánto de la cifra de luz nocturna del área se basa en pocas noches despejadas: la proporción de sus píxeles que la NASA marca como de calidad baja o rellenados con datos anteriores, casi siempre por las nubes.
nightlights.ntl_poor_pct.definition: The share of the area's pixels whose VNP46A3 quality flag is 1 (three or fewer clear observations in the month) or 2 (gap-filled: none), over the pixels with a quality value, pooled over the year's twelve months, in percent.
nightlights.ntl_poor_pct.method: nightlights.py (methods.nightlights): each monthly HDF5 file of tile h11v07 is read with h5py, each pixel goes to the barrio holding its centre, and the year's mean pools the twelve months' pixels with a value.
nightlights.ntl_poor_pct.how_to_read: Puerto Rico in 2025: 0.2%. A high share means the year's mean radiance rests on few clear nights; compare it before reading a change in light.
caveats: Clouds: Puerto Rico is often cloudy, mostly from May to November. A month with few clear nights is flagged poor (three or fewer) or gap-filled (none), and its value can lag the real light.

Moonlight: the product removes moonlight with a model (the lunar BRDF correction), so bright-moon and dark-moon months can be compared; the correction has its own error, largest where the light is dim.

gii.chg.plain: How the updated value compares with the printed 2021 value on the GII's scale: better (green arrow), worse (red arrow), no meaningful change (≈) or not comparable (—). 'Better' follows the index's direction, not a value judgement.
gii.chg.plain_es: Cómo se compara el valor actualizado con el valor publicado de 2021 en la escala del GII: mejor (flecha verde), peor (flecha roja), sin cambio apreciable (≈) o no comparable (—). «Mejor» sigue la dirección del índice; no es un juicio de valor.
gii.chg.definition: chg = 'same' when |upd_value - value| < chg_thr, the threshold: 5% of the interquartile range (inclusive quartiles) of the GII 2026 economies' values for the matching indicator (on the GII's log scale, ln[(max - 1)(x - min)/(max - min) + 1], for the indicators the GII log-transforms: chg_log); otherwise 'better' when (upd_value - value) x dir > 0, else 'worse'. chg = 'na' when the profile has no 2021 value (chg_why 'no_2021', 2.2.3), the two were measured with different sources and definitions (chg_why 'definition': 6.2.1, whose original used the Junta de Planificación's fiscal-year GDP and which the GII 2026 redefined as a five-year average, and 6.2.2), or the source's series changed (chg_why 'series': 2.1.5, UIS's 2024 teacher series), or the method differs from FPR's 2021 one (chg_why 'method': 5.1.1, whose 2021 list of occupations is in FPR's working file, not in the repository; the SOC major groups used now give 29.6% for May 2019 and 30.2% for May 2020, not the printed 32.0). For the WGI (1.1.2, 1.2.1, 1.2.2), whose every release revises all past years, the base is the current release's value for 2018, the data year of the GII 2020 (its Appendix III), not the printed value: chg_base and chg_base_year; the printed value stays as published. chg_delta = upd_value - value (or - chg_base). The arrow points up or down with chg_delta; only the arrow is coloured, and it carries the words as its accessible label.
gii.chg.method: gii.py (change), from the updated value, the printed value and the GII 2026 database extract.
gii.chg.geography: Puerto Rico: the 80 indicators of the Global Innovation Index profile

gii.dir.plain: +1 when a higher value is a better outcome on the GII's scale, -1 when it is worse (the indicators marked *). It sets the colour of the change arrow; it follows the index's method, not a value judgement.
gii.dir.plain_es: +1 cuando un valor más alto es un mejor resultado en la escala del GII, -1 cuando es peor (los indicadores marcados con *). Fija el color de la flecha de cambio; sigue el método del índice, no es un juicio de valor.
gii.dir.definition: -1 for 1.1.1, 1.2.3, 2.1.5 and 4.3.1, the indicators the GII 2020 Appendix III marks as 'higher values indicate worse outcomes' (the profile's *); +1 for the other 76. Checked in the data: in the GII 2020 values of FPR's working file and in the GII 2026 database, the score falls as the value rises for exactly these indicators (Spearman rank correlation below -0.97); the GII 2026 adds two new ones, 3.2.2 (aviation dwell time) and 4.3.2 (industry concentration).

gii.rank_n.definition: 1 + the GII 2020 economies with a value for the indicator, counted in FPR's working file (missing values left out). Only the count is published, not the values.
gii.rank_n.method: Counted on 2026-10-23 in the GII 2020 block of FPR's working file.

gii.changes.plain: What changed in the Global Innovation Index between the GII 2020, the method of FPR's 2021 profile, and the GII 2026: the editions, the method, the indicators that changed and the new ones, with whether Puerto Rico data exist.
gii.changes.plain_es: Qué cambió en el Índice Global de Innovación entre el GII 2020, el método del perfil de FPR de 2021, y el GII 2026: las ediciones, el método, los indicadores que cambiaron y los nuevos, con si hay datos de Puerto Rico.
gii.changes.definition: editions: economies, indicators, pillars and sub-pillars of the GII 2020, 2025 and 2026, each with its source; method: the changes in normalization, outlier treatment, weights, coverage, ranks and direction, in English and Spanish, each with its source; crosswalk: the 80 indicators of 2020 with the GII 2026 code and the status (same, renamed, redefined, dropped; their notes are in gii_profile.json's texts); new_2026: the 16 new indicators of the GII 2026 with their source, whether Puerto Rico data exist (yes, no, an FPR estimate possible, an FPR estimate given, proprietary, not verified) and n, the GII 2026 economies with data; for IN.3.3.2 (low-carbon energy use) pr_est holds FPR's estimate: the US EIA's consumption from nuclear, renewables and other as a % of Puerto Rico's total energy consumption, with its year, series, link and source, and no GII 2026 position; sources: the WIPO pages and files, with the date checked.
gii.changes.method: gii.py, from docs/analysis/gii-2021/gii_crosswalk.json, the GII 2026 database extract and, for the FPR estimate of IN.3.3.2, the US EIA's bulk file INTL.zip.
gii.changes.geography: Puerto Rico: the 80 indicators of the Global Innovation Index profile

gii.file.plain: FPR's 2021 Global Innovation Index profile of Puerto Rico, kept as printed, with the newest open value of each indicator that can be updated, an arrow that says whether it is better or worse than in 2021 on the GII's scale, the indicator's status in the GII 2026 and, where the sources match, an indicative position among the GII 2026 economies. FPR's calculation, not an official ranking.
gii.file.plain_es: El perfil de Puerto Rico de FPR de 2021 en el Índice Global de Innovación, tal como se publicó, con el valor abierto más reciente de cada indicador que se puede actualizar, una flecha que dice si es mejor o peor que en 2021 en la escala del GII, el estado del indicador en el GII 2026 y, donde las fuentes coinciden, una posición indicativa entre las economías del GII 2026. Cálculo de FPR, no una clasificación oficial.
gii.file.definition: One record for each of the 80 indicators of the GII 2020 framework (7 pillars, 21 sub-pillars), with the fields gii.*: the 2021 value, rank and marks (frozen), the updated value with its year, source and kind, and the GII 2026 comparison. The pillars block holds the names and descriptions; the texts block holds each indicator's name, definition, FPR method note, corrections and reason for no update, in English and Spanish; the sources block names the update sources; about counts the updated and compared indicators.
gii.file.method: docs/analysis/gii-2021/gii_original.json is the profile frozen as printed (written once on 2026-10-23); gii.py reads it, fetches the open series (World Bank WGI and WDI, UNESCO UIS, IMF, BLS LAUS and OEWS, US EIA, Census Bureau population estimates; none needs an API key) into cache/gii/, takes the freshest candidate of each, and places the updated value among the GII 2026 economies for the indicators whose source and definition match.
gii.file.how_to_read: Read the 2021 value and rank together. The updated value is not ranked among the GII 2020 economies; its arrow compares it with the 2021 value in the direction of the index. A position X/N among the GII 2026 economies is indicative. No overall, sub-index or pillar score exists for Puerto Rico.
caveats: Puerto Rico is not in the official Global Innovation Index; the ranks are FPR's.
The printed ranks are out of 132 even where fewer economies had data (rank_n).
Proprietary 2021 values (IHS Markit, Web of Science, Brand Finance) are not updated.
Sources revise past years (WGI, UIS, IMF), so an updated value is not a change from the printed one.
gii.file.geography: Puerto Rico: the 80 indicators of the Global Innovation Index profile

gii.components.plain_es: En los dos índices compuestos de TIC (3.1.1 y 3.1.2), los valores más recientes de sus componentes principales del Banco Mundial, como contexto; no son un valor nuevo del índice.
gii.components.definition: A list of {series, value, year}: fixed telephone and mobile subscriptions per 100 people (3.1.1), individuals using the internet (%) and fixed broadband subscriptions per 100 people (3.1.2).

gii.c26_pos.plain: Where Puerto Rico's updated value would fall among the GII 2026 economies with data, written c26_pos/c26_of like the profile's ranks. Indicative position calculated by FPR, not an official WIPO rank.
gii.c26_pos.plain_es: Dónde quedaría el valor actualizado de Puerto Rico entre las economías del GII 2026 con datos, escrito c26_pos/c26_of como las posiciones del perfil. Posición indicativa calculada por FPR, no oficial de la OMPI.
gii.c26_pos.definition: c26_pos = 1 + the number of GII 2026 economies whose screened value is strictly better than Puerto Rico's (lower is better where c26_lower_better), so ties share the better place, as WIPO's own ranks do (true for 78 of the 79 indicators of the GII 2026 database); c26_of = the economies with data + 1. Ranking the value gives the place the 0-100 score would give, because min-max and the log transform keep the order; no position is given where the GII winsorizes and Puerto Rico's value lies beyond the capped values. For the 10 indicators whose Puerto Rico source and definition match (COMPARE in gii.py): 1.1.2, 1.2.1, 1.2.2, 2.1.1, 2.1.3, 2.2.1, 2.2.2, 2.2.3, 3.2.3 and 4.3.3. 2.1.5, 4.3.1, 6.2.1 and 6.2.2 get none (NO_POSITION gives the reason in each open row).
gii.c26_pos.method: gii.py, from the extract of the GII 2026 database (cache/gii/2026/).

gii.upd_kind.plain: 'official' when the value is the source's own figure; 'fpr' when FPR's method was applied to open data (shown as 'FPR estimate'). upd_estimate marks a UIS estimate.

gii.c26_pr_value.plain_es: El valor de Puerto Rico que se ubica entre las economías del GII 2026, y su año, que depende del indicador: el año del GII 2026 en las puntuaciones de gobernanza y el PIB, un promedio de tres años en la formación bruta de capital, el año más reciente de Puerto Rico en los indicadores de la UNESCO.

economy.hh_income_75k_plus_pct.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many had a yearly income of $75,000 or more. The dollars are those of the last year of the survey window. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 14.0% in 2020-2024.
economy.hh_income_75k_plus_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos tuvieron un ingreso anual de $75,000 o más. Los dólares son los del último año del periodo de la encuesta. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 14.0% en 2020-2024.
economy.hh_income_75k_plus_pct.definition: Households with income of $75,000 or more in the past 12 months, divided by all households, times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B19001. The top is the sum of cells 13 to 17 ($75,000 to $99,999, $100,000 to $124,999, $125,000 to $149,999, $150,000 to $199,999 and $200,000 or more). The bottom is cell 1, all households. Household income is the money income of all household members aged 15 or over, before taxes.
economy.hh_income_75k_plus_pct.method: The observatory reads table B19001 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 13 to 17 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.hh_income_75k_plus_pct.how_to_read: A value of 14 means that 14 of every 100 households had income of $75,000 or more. It counts households, not people, and does not adjust for household size. Use it with the share under $25,000 to see both ends of the income spread. Income here is money income from all regular sources, such as wages, self-employment, Social Security, retirement and public assistance. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months), cells 13 to 17 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The dollars are those of the last year of each window. The Census Bureau states table B19001 in inflation-adjusted dollars of that year (its table title says 2010 dollars for the 2006-2010 window and 2020 dollars for the 2016-2020 window), so the $75,000 line means 2010 dollars in the 2006-2010 window and 2024 dollars in the 2020-2024 window. The observatory changes nothing between windows, and percent layers on the Analysis tab have no inflation switch. In the 2026-10 snapshot, part of the rise from 7.0% (2006-2010) to 14.0% (2020-2024) comes from the fixed dollar line, not from real income. By the US Consumer Price Index (CPI-U), US city average (annual averages 218.056 in 2010 and 313.689 in 2024), $75,000 in 2024 dollars is about $52,100 in 2010 dollars. The observatory uses only the US city average CPI-U, so this is an approximation for Puerto Rico, and the factor the Census Bureau used to express the survey dollars may differ. The fixed line is therefore a lower real amount in later windows, which raises the share above it even if real incomes did not change.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.9 to ±7.7 points across the 78 municipalities, and 26 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate. The shares are small, so a margin of a point or two matters.
A value near zero is a survey result for a small sample. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Las Marías shows 2.0% (± 1.5 points) for 2020-2024.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 9.6% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 14.0%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Moca goes from 6.38% (2017-2021) to 10.71% (2018-2022). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
economy.hh_income_75k_plus_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months, in inflation-adjusted dollars), cells 001 and 013-017; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). CPI-U, US city average (series CUUR0000SA0), used only to illustrate the fixed dollar line.

economy.hh_income_under_25k_pct.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many had a yearly income below $25,000. The dollars are those of the last year of the survey window. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 48.2% in 2020-2024.
economy.hh_income_under_25k_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos tuvieron un ingreso anual menor de $25,000. Los dólares son los del último año del periodo de la encuesta. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 48.2% en 2020-2024.
economy.hh_income_under_25k_pct.definition: Households with income below $25,000 in the past 12 months, divided by all households, times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B19001. The top is the sum of cells 2 to 5 (under $10,000, $10,000 to $14,999, $15,000 to $19,999 and $20,000 to $24,999). The bottom is cell 1, all households. Household income is the money income of all household members aged 15 or over, before taxes.
economy.hh_income_under_25k_pct.method: The observatory reads table B19001 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 2 to 5 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.hh_income_under_25k_pct.how_to_read: A value of 48 means that 48 of every 100 households had income below $25,000. It counts households, not people, and does not adjust for household size. It is not the poverty rate; for that, see 'Population below the poverty level' (housing.poverty_pct). Income here is money income from all regular sources, such as wages, self-employment, Social Security, retirement and public assistance. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months), cells 2 to 5 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The dollars are those of the last year of each window. The Census Bureau states table B19001 in inflation-adjusted dollars of that year (its table title says 2010 dollars for the 2006-2010 window and 2020 dollars for the 2016-2020 window), so the $25,000 line means 2010 dollars in the 2006-2010 window and 2024 dollars in the 2020-2024 window. The observatory changes nothing between windows, and percent layers on the Analysis tab have no inflation switch. In the 2026-10 snapshot, part of the fall from 60.1% (2006-2010) to 48.2% (2020-2024) comes from the fixed dollar line, not from real income. By the US Consumer Price Index (CPI-U), US city average (annual averages 218.056 in 2010 and 313.689 in 2024), $25,000 in 2024 dollars is about $17,400 in 2010 dollars. The observatory uses only the US city average CPI-U, so this is an approximation for Puerto Rico, and the factor the Census Bureau used to express the survey dollars may differ. The fixed line is therefore a lower real amount in later windows, which lowers the share below it even if real incomes did not change.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±1.1 to ±12.3 points across the 78 municipalities, and 1 of the 78 is larger than 30% of the estimate.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 51.7% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 48.2%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra goes from 48.10% (2018-2022) to 39.02% (2019-2023). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
economy.hh_income_under_25k_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B19001 (Household Income in the Past 12 Months, in inflation-adjusted dollars), cells 001 and 002-005; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). CPI-U, US city average (series CUUR0000SA0), used only to illustrate the fixed dollar line.

economy.gini.plain: A number from 0 to 1 that shows how unevenly household income is spread in the area. 0 means every household has the same income; 1 means one household has all of it. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 0.543 in 2020-2024.
economy.gini.plain_es: Un número de 0 a 1 que muestra cuán desigual es la distribución del ingreso de los hogares en el área. 0 significa que todos los hogares tienen el mismo ingreso; 1 significa que un solo hogar lo tiene todo. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 0.543 en 2020-2024.
economy.gini.definition: The Gini index of household income, as the Census Bureau publishes it (American Community Survey, ACS, table B19083, cell 1; universe: households). Household income is the money income of all household members aged 15 or over in the past 12 months, before taxes: wages, self-employment, interest, Social Security, retirement, public assistance and similar regular sources. Capital gains and non-cash benefits are left out. The index runs from 0 (every household has the same income) to 1 (one household has all the income).
economy.gini.method: The observatory reads table B19083 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. The estimate and its margin of error are the Census Bureau's published values (cell 1), rounded to three decimals. No calculation is added.
economy.gini.how_to_read: A higher value means income is more unevenly spread. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 78 municipalities run from 0.369 to 0.629 for 2020-2024. Compare places within one window and check the margin of error. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in the index's own units, for example ±0.035. To cite the source number, give the table, the window and the place, for example: 'US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B19083 (Gini Index of Income Inequality), Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' If you took the number from the observatory, also cite Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory.
caveats: It measures how unequal incomes are inside one place, not how high they are. Two places with the same Gini can have very different incomes. For the level, see median household income.
It compares households, not people, and does not adjust for household size.

Margins are wide for small municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.010 to ±0.117 across the 78 municipalities (Culebra 0.369, ± 0.046; Dorado 0.629, ± 0.035). Small differences between municipalities are within the margins.
Unlike dollar amounts, the index is a ratio, so it does not depend on the year of the dollars and needs no inflation adjustment to compare windows.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's estimate for the whole island, not an average of the 78 municipal values. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 0.492 for 2020-2024 and the island value is 0.543.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the index a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Sabana Grande goes from 0.467 (2018-2022) to 0.563 (2019-2023). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 20% of barrios and 1% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
economy.gini.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (island total); also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts
economy.gini.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B19083 (Gini Index of Income Inequality), cell 001; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

housing.median_hh_income.plain: The middle household income in the area: half of households earn more, half earn less. Puerto Rico: $26,297 a year in the 2020-2024 window, in 2024 dollars.
housing.median_hh_income.plain_es: El ingreso del hogar que queda en el medio en el área: la mitad de los hogares gana más y la mitad gana menos. Puerto Rico: $26,297 al año en la ventana 2020-2024, en dólares de 2024.
housing.median_hh_income.definition: Median income of all households in the past 12 months (American Community Survey, ACS, table B19013, cell 1). Household income adds the income of every household member aged 15 or over. Income means money income before taxes from wages, self-employment, interest, Social Security, retirement, public assistance and similar regular sources; it leaves out capital gains and non-cash benefits.
housing.median_hh_income.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. The value and its margin of error are the Census Bureau's published ones. It is also the income used for the maximum affordable loan and the affordability ratio.
housing.median_hh_income.how_to_read: Compare it with the cost of housing, not with a single person's pay: one household can have several earners or none. For income per person, see per capita income. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window (2024 dollars for 2020-2024), as the Census Bureau states them. Amounts from different windows are not in the same dollars. To compare across windows, use the Analysis tab's Inflation-adjusted option, which restates dollars with the US Consumer Price Index (see the entry on inflation adjustment).

From 2010 to 2024 the US Consumer Price Index (CPI-U) annual average rose 43.9% (annual average index values: 218.056 in 2010 and 313.689 in 2024). This median rose 40%, from $18,791 to $26,297, so it is not a rise in buying power by that index.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
A median hides the spread: it says nothing about how many households earn very little or very much.

Estimates for small municipalities are imprecise. The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.

The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 49% of barrios and 36% of census tracts that have a value. A median at the edge of an open-ended interval (the Census Bureau prints the boundary) or equal to 0 is not an estimate and is left empty (1 barrio and 4 census tracts in 2020-2024). See methods.small_area_estimates.
housing.median_hh_income.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts
housing.median_hh_income.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B19013 (Median Household Income in the Past 12 Months), cell 001; windows 2006-2010 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b19013.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition). CPI-U, US city average (series CUUR0000SA0), used only for the price comparison in the caveats.

municipalities.median_hh_income.plain: The middle yearly income of households in the municipality. Half of the households earn more and half earn less.
municipalities.median_hh_income.plain_es: El ingreso anual del medio de los hogares del municipio. La mitad de los hogares gana más y la mitad gana menos.
municipalities.median_hh_income.definition: Median household income in the past 12 months, table B19013 of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). A household is all the people who live in one housing unit. Its income adds the money income of every member aged 15 or over. The Census Bureau reports ACS dollar amounts in the dollars of the last year of the window (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot; the Analysis tab says the same). The observatory applies no inflation adjustment.
municipalities.median_hh_income.method: Copied unchanged from ACS table B19013, cell 001 (file acsdt5y2024-b19013.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot). The same table for the 2008-2012 window feeds income_change_pct. The value is also the input of max_affordable_loan.
municipalities.median_hh_income.how_to_read: A higher value means a typical household in the municipality has more money to spend. It describes households, not individuals. For income per person see 'Per capita income' in the Housing page series.
caveats: It is money income before taxes. It does not count the value of benefits that are not paid in cash.
'Past 12 months' means the 12 months before each household was interviewed. The window pools interviews from five years, so it is not one calendar year.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±$805 (Mayagüez) to ±$7,604 (Culebra). The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.

The 2008-2012 value is in 2012 dollars, not in the dollars of this field, so do not subtract one from the other as if the dollars were the same. 'Change in median household income since 2008-2012 (%)' compares them as published, so it includes general price rises.

housing.median_owner_income.plain: The middle income of households that own their home. Half of owner households earn more, half less. Puerto Rico: $32,125 a year in the 2020-2024 window, in 2024 dollars.
housing.median_owner_income.plain_es: El ingreso del medio de los hogares que son dueños de su vivienda. La mitad de los hogares propietarios gana más y la mitad, menos. Puerto Rico: $32,125 al año en la ventana 2020-2024, en dólares de 2024.
housing.median_owner_income.definition: Median household income in the past 12 months of owner-occupied housing units (American Community Survey, ACS, table B25119, cell 2, Median Household Income by Tenure). Income means money income before taxes from wages, self-employment, interest, Social Security, retirement, public assistance and similar regular sources; it leaves out capital gains and non-cash benefits.
housing.median_owner_income.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. housing.median_owner_income.how_to_read: Tenure means whether a household owns or rents its home. It describes the home, not the person: a household is an owner household if someone in it owns or is buying the home. The Census Bureau groups it by the householder, the person in whose name the home is owned or rented. Read it with renter household income to see the gap between the two groups. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window (2024 dollars for 2020-2024), as the Census Bureau states them. Amounts from different windows are not in the same dollars. housing.per_capita_income.plain: Total income of everyone in the area divided by the number of people, children included. It is an average, so high earners lift it. Puerto Rico: $17,981 a year in the 2020-2024 window, in 2024 dollars.
housing.per_capita_income.plain_es: El ingreso total de todas las personas del área dividido entre el número de personas, incluidos los menores. Es un promedio, así que los ingresos altos lo suben. Puerto Rico: $17,981 al año en la ventana 2020-2024, en dólares de 2024.
housing.per_capita_income.definition: Mean income per person in the past 12 months (American Community Survey, ACS, table B19301, cell 1): the total income of all people 15 and over divided by the total population of all ages. Income means money income before taxes from wages, self-employment, interest, Social Security, retirement, public assistance and similar regular sources; it leaves out capital gains and non-cash benefits.
housing.per_capita_income.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. The value and its margin of error are the Census Bureau's published ones.
housing.per_capita_income.how_to_read: It is lower than median household income mainly because a household's income is shared by about 2.5 people on average (2.48 in Puerto Rico in 2020-2024), and because it is a mean per person that includes children and people with no income. Do not compare the two as if they described the same unit. Do not use it to say what a typical person earns; it is a mean, and a few high incomes raise it. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Dollars are those of the last year of each five-year window (2024 dollars for 2020-2024), as the Census Bureau states them. Amounts from different windows are not in the same dollars. To compare across windows, use the Analysis tab's Inflation-adjusted option, which restates dollars with the US Consumer Price Index (see the entry on inflation adjustment).

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
A mean is pulled up by high incomes. The median household income is the better guide to a typical household.

housing.poverty_pct.plain: Out of every 100 people the Census Bureau could classify, how many lived with income below the poverty level in the past 12 months. In Puerto Rico it was 40.5% in the 2020-2024 window.
housing.poverty_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas que el Negociado del Censo pudo clasificar, cuántas vivieron con un ingreso por debajo del nivel de pobreza en los últimos 12 meses. En Puerto Rico fue 40.5% en la ventana 2020-2024.
housing.poverty_pct.definition: People whose income in the past 12 months was below the Census Bureau's poverty level (American Community Survey, ACS, table B17001, cell 2) divided by all people for whom the Bureau determines poverty status (B17001, cell 1), times 100. The Bureau does not determine poverty status for people in institutions such as prisons and nursing homes, in military group quarters or in college dormitories, or for unrelated children under 15. The poverty level depends on family size and the ages of its members, not on local prices.
housing.poverty_pct.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 2 by cell 1. The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator. Puerto Rico's value comes from the island row of the same table.
housing.poverty_pct.how_to_read: A value of 40 means that 40 of every 100 counted people lived below the poverty level. It counts people, not households, and it does not show how far below the line people are or for how long. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
Income is measured over the 12 months before each household was surveyed, and interviews are spread across the five years of a window, so a window blends different years.
The poverty level is a national threshold. It is not adjusted for the cost of living in Puerto Rico.

The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities. The Housing page also prints the median of the 78 municipalities above each chart, which is a different number.

See methods.small_area_estimates.

municipalities.poverty_pct.plain: Out of every 100 people, how many live in a family with income below the federal poverty level. The Census Bureau compares the family's income with a threshold for its size. A person with no relatives is compared on their own income. People whose poverty status the Bureau cannot determine are left out.
municipalities.poverty_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas, cuántas viven en una familia con un ingreso por debajo del nivel federal de pobreza. El Negociado del Censo compara el ingreso de la familia con un umbral según su tamaño. A una persona sin parientes se le compara su propio ingreso. Se excluyen las personas cuya condición de pobreza el Negociado no puede determinar.
municipalities.poverty_pct.definition: People whose income in the past 12 months is below the poverty threshold, divided by the population for whom poverty status is determined, times 100. The Census Bureau compares the total income of a person's family (or, for a person with no relatives in the household, the person's own income) with the federal threshold for that family size. From table B17001 (cells 002 and 001) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
municipalities.poverty_pct.method: B17001 cell 002 divided by cell 001, times 100, rounded to one decimal (file acsdt5y2024-b17001.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot).
municipalities.poverty_pct.how_to_read: A high value means a large share of residents live on very low incomes by the federal definition. It counts people, not households.
caveats: The poverty level is a federal threshold that depends on family size and does not vary by place, so it does not reflect local prices.
'Past 12 months' means the 12 months before each household was interviewed. The window pools interviews from five years, so it is not one calendar year.
The base leaves out some people in group quarters, such as prisons, nursing homes, military barracks and college dormitories.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±1.1 points (San Juan) to ±9.5 points (Culebra). The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.

economy.accommodation_jobs.plain: Private jobs at hotels, resorts, inns and other places to stay in the municipality. Many municipalities show a blank because the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) hides the figure to protect an employer's privacy, or publishes no figure for them. A blank is not zero.
economy.accommodation_jobs.plain_es: Empleos privados en hoteles, complejos turísticos, posadas y otros lugares de hospedaje en el municipio. Muchos municipios aparecen en blanco porque el BLS (Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales) oculta la cifra para proteger la privacidad de un patrono, o no publica cifras para ellos. Un espacio en blanco no es cero.
economy.accommodation_jobs.definition: Average private-sector jobs in industry group 721, accommodation, of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), at employers located in the municipality. It includes hotels and motels (casino hotels too), resorts, inns, guesthouses, bed-and-breakfasts, recreational-vehicle parks and camps, and rooming houses. It is a part of sector 72, accommodation and food services. Hosts who rent out a home and have no employees are not counted. The data come from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
economy.accommodation_jobs.method: Column annual_avg_emplvl of the BLS annual file, ownership code 5 (private), industry code 721. A row that BLS marks as withheld is left blank, and a municipality with no row is also blank.
economy.accommodation_jobs.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island figure fell from 15,291 in 2014 to 8,525 in 2020 and recovered to 14,947 in 2025. In 2024 the largest published municipal values are Carolina (1,369), Dorado (1,198), Ponce (1,031). In 2024 the municipal values add up to only 40% of the island figure; BLS hid San Juan's value that year (4,983 jobs in 2023) and other cells too. They add up to 72% in 2014 and 63% in 2025. Do not rank municipalities by this variable without checking which ones are blank.
caveats: A blank means that BLS withheld the figure or published no row. It is not zero. The published data do not tell the two apart.
BLS hides a cell when it could identify one employer, which is easy where a municipality has only a few hotels. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan, the largest municipality, is hidden in 2024 only.
Short-term rentals offered by individual hosts are not counted. Only employers with employees under unemployment insurance are. This is employment at those employers, not rental listings or beds.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 29 municipalities have the sector 72 total published for 2024 and accommodation blank; in 19 of them food service is blank too, so neither part can be worked out from the total.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 has fewer published values than any earlier year (13 municipalities, against 15 in 2024), and it is preliminary.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 78 municipalities, 17 have a value in 2014, 34 are withheld and 27 have no row; in 2024 the counts are 15, 41 and 22; in 2025 they are 13, 45 and 20. From 2014 to 2024, between 34 and 41 municipalities are withheld each year and between 22 and 27 have no row.

economy.food_service_jobs.plain: Private jobs at restaurants, fast-food outlets, cafes, bars and caterers in the municipality. The figure is blank where it is withheld.
economy.food_service_jobs.plain_es: Empleos privados en restaurantes, establecimientos de comida rápida, cafeterías, barras y servicios de catering en el municipio. La cifra aparece en blanco donde se retiene.
economy.food_service_jobs.definition: Average private-sector jobs in industry group 722, food services and drinking places, of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), at employers located in the municipality. It includes full-service restaurants, fast-food and counter-service outlets, cafeterias, coffee and snack shops, bars, food trucks and caterers. It is a part of sector 72, accommodation and food services. The data come from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
economy.food_service_jobs.method: Column annual_avg_emplvl of the BLS annual file, ownership code 5 (private), industry code 722. A row that BLS marks as withheld is left blank.
economy.food_service_jobs.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island figure rose from 61,116 in 2014 to 78,341 in 2025, with a dip to 54,827 in 2020. In 2024 the largest published municipal values are Carolina (5,527), Ponce (4,047), Caguas (3,700). The municipal values add up to 50% of the island figure in 2024 (74% in 2014, 68% in 2025); 2024 is low because BLS hid San Juan's value that year (18,054 jobs in 2023). Restaurants serve residents as well as visitors, so this is not a count of visitor jobs.
caveats: A blank means that BLS withheld the figure; it is not zero. In the 2026-10 snapshot, BLS publishes a food service row for every municipality in every year, so a blank is a withheld cell, not a missing industry.
Food trucks and food stands run by an owner with no paid employees are not counted.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, only 29 municipalities have a value in 2025, against 42 in 2024, so the 2025 map has far fewer values. The change is mostly in what BLS hides, not in the industry.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's value is hidden in 2024 although its sector 72 total is published.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 78 municipalities, 44 have a value in 2014 and 34 are withheld; in 2024 the counts are 42 and 36; in 2025 they are 29 and 49. From 2014 to 2024, between 29 and 36 municipalities are withheld each year.

economy.industry_hhi.plain: A score of how concentrated the local jobs are in a few industries. A low score means jobs are spread across many industries; a high score means a few, often government, hold most of them.
economy.industry_hhi.plain_es: Una puntuación de qué tan concentrados están los empleos locales en pocas industrias. Una puntuación baja significa que los empleos se reparten entre muchas industrias; una alta significa que unas pocas, a menudo el gobierno, tienen la mayoría.
economy.industry_hhi.definition: The Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI) of the job shares of the municipality's industries. Each industry's share of all local jobs is squared and the squares are added and multiplied by 10,000. The industries are the 19 private sectors of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) that the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes for the municipality, plus government as one group. It is calculated only where the published sectors and government cover at least 80% of all jobs. It is also blank where private jobs are withheld, because government jobs cannot then be worked out.
economy.industry_hhi.method: Calculated by the observatory. For each municipality and year: total jobs T = qcew_jobs. Government G = total jobs minus private jobs. Each published private sector gives S, its jobs. The sectors and government are 'covered' if (sum of S + G) / T is at least 0.8. If so, HHI = round(10,000 x sum of (jobs / T)^2) over the published sectors and government; the shares are of all jobs, including government, and a hidden sector adds nothing. If not, the value is blank. It can be recomputed from the published sector values. The value is also blank where private jobs are withheld, because government jobs cannot then be worked out. The Analysis tab's inspector also names the largest employer group (see its entry). That group uses the same sector values but has no 80% test.
economy.industry_hhi.how_to_read: Lower is more diversified. With jobs spread evenly over the 20 groups the score is 500; with all jobs in one group it is 10,000. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 municipal values run from 814 (Guaynabo) to 5,940 (Maunabo), and the island value is 1,040 (built from all 19 sectors). A high value can come from one large private sector or from a large government share, because government counts as one group. The score compares places and years within this data. It is not a measure of economic health. The inspector's 'largest employer group' ignores hidden sectors and counts government as one group, so it can name Government or a smaller sector when a larger sector is withheld; see its entry.
caveats: Government is treated as one group. A municipality where government holds most jobs scores high mainly for that reason. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Maunabo has the highest value in 2024, with a government share of 76%.

Jobs in hidden sectors are left out, so a score can be too low but not too high, compared with a calculation that had every sector. Up to 20% of jobs can be missing from the calculation, because of the 80% rule.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, many municipalities have no value: 19 in 2014, 30 in 2024 and 38 in 2025. A municipality can enter or leave the set from one year to the next as BLS hides or shows sectors, so do not read a change that comes with a change in the set of published sectors as a trend.
It uses only 20 groups, and the private sectors are broad. It does not see concentration inside a sector, such as one large employer.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island value uses all 19 sectors except in 2015 (sector 81 missing), 2022 (sector 51 missing) and 2025 (five sectors missing: mining, utilities, construction, transportation and warehousing, information). In 2025 the published sectors and government cover 91.8% of jobs, and with those five sectors held at their 2024 size the score would be about 1,026, not 1,004. In 2015 and 2022 the gap is about 3 points. 2024 is the latest island value built from all 19 sectors, so do not read the 2024 to 2025 island change as a trend.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, among the 48 municipalities with a value in 2024, smaller ones tend to score higher: the rank correlation with total jobs is about -0.63 (-1 would mean the order is exactly reversed). The 30 municipalities without a value tend to be small (median 3,036 jobs, against 7,084 for those with a value). A high score is not by itself a sign of a weak economy.

Do not compare a municipality's score with the island's. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island figure has almost every sector published in every year; a municipality often does not, and a score built from fewer sectors is lower.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island value exists in every year. Culebra's value is blank in 2015 to 2021 because its private jobs are withheld, and in 2022 to 2025 because the published sectors and government cover less than 80% of its jobs.

economy.top_sector.plain: The industry, or government, that holds the most jobs in a municipality in a given year, among the groups the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes there. The Analysis tab shows it, with its share of all local jobs, when you select a municipality.
economy.top_sector.plain_es: La industria, o el gobierno, que tiene más empleos en un municipio en un año dado, entre los grupos que el BLS (Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales) publica allí. La pestaña Análisis lo muestra, junto con su proporción de todos los empleos locales, al seleccionar un municipio.
economy.top_sector.definition: For each place and year, the group with the most jobs among the 19 private sectors of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) that the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes for that place, with government taken as one group. The jobs come from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW). The data hold three items for each place and year: the group's name, its share of all jobs (private and government) in percent with one decimal, and the share of the place's private jobs that sit in published sectors, as a whole percent.
economy.top_sector.method: Calculated by the observatory together with the industry concentration index. For each place and year where total jobs and private jobs are published, it takes the jobs of each published private sector and of government (total jobs minus private jobs) and keeps the group with the most jobs. Share of all jobs = group jobs / total jobs x 100, rounded to 1 decimal. Share of private jobs in published sectors = sum of the published private sector jobs / private jobs x 100, rounded to a whole number. Unlike the concentration index, it has no 80% test. It is published in economy_series.json under extras.top_sector, a list per year in the same order as the places. The Analysis tab inspector shows the name and the share of all jobs.
economy.top_sector.how_to_read: Read it as the biggest group among those BLS shows. Government counts as one group and the private sectors as 19, so Government is often the largest. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Government is named for 49 of the 78 municipalities in 2024, and for Puerto Rico (20.3% of jobs in 2025).
caveats: A group that BLS hides cannot be named, so the true largest group can be a hidden sector. For example, in the 2026-10 snapshot, Government is named for Maricao in 2024 with 30.1% of jobs, but the published sectors hold only 20% of its private jobs, so a hidden sector could be larger.
The percentage is the group's share of all jobs, government included. It is not a share of private jobs.
It has no 80% test, unlike the industry concentration index, so it is shown even where most private jobs are in hidden sectors.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, every place has a value in every year except Culebra in 2015 to 2021, when its private jobs are withheld (941 of 948 place-years, Puerto Rico included).

economy.top_sector.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files (see the QCEW method entry). Rows: own_code 5 for the 19 sectors, plus own_code 0 and own_code 5 with industry_code 10 for total and government jobs.

economy.tourism_jobs.plain: Private jobs in hotels, restaurants, bars, arts and recreation in the municipality. Statisticians use it as a stand-in for the visitor economy. It also counts restaurants that serve residents.
economy.tourism_jobs.plain_es: Empleos privados en hoteles, restaurantes, barras, artes y recreación en el municipio. En estadística se usa como indicador aproximado de la economía del visitante. También cuenta los restaurantes que atienden a residentes.
economy.tourism_jobs.definition: Private jobs at employers located in the municipality in two sectors of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS): accommodation and food services (sector 72) plus arts, entertainment and recreation (sector 71). The figures come from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Where BLS withholds sector 71 for a municipality, only sector 72 is counted, so the value is slightly low there. Where BLS withholds sector 72, the value is blank.
economy.tourism_jobs.method: Calculated by the observatory: sector 72 jobs plus sector 71 jobs where sector 71 has a published value; sector 72 jobs alone where sector 71 is withheld or has no row. If sector 72 is withheld the value is blank, even when sector 71 or the parts of sector 72 (721 and 722) are published. The value exists wherever sector 72 has a value.
economy.tourism_jobs.how_to_read: It measures jobs in the industries that visitors use. It does not say how many of the customers are visitors. The Analysis tab's Tourism economy view shows it as a share of the municipality's jobs. In the 2026-10 snapshot, tourism-related jobs are 10.5% of island jobs in 2025 (99,477), up from 8.8% in 2014. In 2024, the highest shares of local jobs among the municipalities with a value are Rincón (33%), Río Grande (31%), Vieques (26%) and Dorado (26%).
caveats: Residents eat out and use recreation too, so part of these jobs serve residents, not visitors.

Visitor-serving jobs in other sectors are not included: air and ground transport, retail, travel agencies and tour operators, and vacation-rental management companies. Hosts who rent a home and have no employees are not counted at all.

economy.qcew_avg_pay.plain: What the average job at an employer in the municipality paid in the year, in dollars of that year. It describes the jobs located there, not the incomes of the people who live there.
economy.qcew_avg_pay.plain_es: Lo que pagó en el año el empleo promedio en un patrono del municipio, en dólares de ese año. Describe los empleos ubicados allí, no los ingresos de las personas que viven allí.
economy.qcew_avg_pay.definition: Total annual wages divided by average jobs, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). It is a mean per job, not a median. It is not converted to full-time equivalents, so part-time and part-year jobs lower it. It includes private and government jobs and is in US dollars of the year, not adjusted for inflation.
economy.qcew_avg_pay.method: Column avg_annual_pay of the BLS annual file, ownership code 0, industry code 10; the observatory reads it as published and does not compute it.
economy.qcew_avg_pay.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island average rose from $27,097 in 2014 to $36,419 in 2025. Juncos has the highest average pay in every year from 2014 to 2025 ($60,788 in 2025). The lowest is Las Marías in 2025 ($21,351). A high value means the jobs located there pay more on average; it can reflect the mix of industries, and it does not mean that residents earn more. For the income of residents, use the household income variables.
caveats: Dollars are not adjusted. In the 2026-10 snapshot, using the US consumer price index (CPI-U, US city average, an approximation because the observatory's sources hold no Puerto Rico index), the 2025 island average is worth about $26,800 in 2014 dollars, close to the $27,097 of 2014.
It is a mean, so a few very high pay packages raise it in a small municipality.
It is pay per job, not per hour or per person. A part-time job counts as one job.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 78 municipalities have a value in every year. In the observatory's file, total wages divided by jobs differs from the published average by no more than $24 in any municipality or year, probably because BLS rounds the job counts it publishes.
economy.qcew_avg_pay.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island figure is published by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, not summed from the 78)
economy.qcew_avg_pay.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Row: own_code 0, industry_code 10, column avg_annual_pay. Inflation comparison: BLS CPI-U, US city average (annual average).

economy.qcew_estabs.plain: How many work sites with paid employees are located in the municipality, averaged over the year. One firm with ten stores counts as ten.
economy.qcew_estabs.plain_es: Cuántos lugares de trabajo con personal asalariado están ubicados en el municipio, en promedio durante el año. Una empresa con diez tiendas cuenta como diez.
economy.qcew_estabs.definition: Average number of establishments in the year, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). An establishment is one work site of an employer, such as a store, an office or a plant. The annual figure is the average of the four quarterly counts. Private and government work sites with employees under unemployment insurance are included.
economy.qcew_estabs.method: Column annual_avg_estabs of the BLS annual file, ownership code 0, industry code 10. The island value is BLS's own figure, not the sum of the 78 municipalities.
economy.qcew_estabs.how_to_read: Divide jobs by establishments to get the average size of a work site. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island average is 18.0 jobs per site in 2025 (947,557 jobs, 52,582 sites). It counts sites, not companies or businesses: a chain with 30 stores counts 30 times. A person who works alone and has no employees is not counted.
caveats: Counts work sites, not firms. The number of firms is not in this data.
Only sites that report employees to unemployment insurance are counted. Sole proprietors and informal businesses are not.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island count rose from 46,942 in 2014 to 52,582 in 2025 (12.0% higher).
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 78 municipalities have a value in every year. BLS's island figure is above the sum of the 78 municipalities by 318 (0.7%) in 2014 and by 541 (1.0%) in 2025.

economy.qcew_gov_jobs.plain: How many jobs in the municipality are with federal, Commonwealth or municipal government, averaged over the year. It is total jobs minus private jobs.
economy.qcew_gov_jobs.plain_es: Cuántos empleos en el municipio son del gobierno federal, del gobierno central o de los municipios, en promedio durante el año. Es el total de empleos menos los empleos privados.
economy.qcew_gov_jobs.definition: Total jobs minus private-sector jobs for the same municipality and year. It is the jobs at government employers located in the municipality: federal, Commonwealth (state) and municipal, including municipal agencies and public schools. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reports these jobs under ownership codes 1 (federal), 2 (state) and 3 (local) in the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW); the observatory publishes only the total.
economy.qcew_gov_jobs.method: Calculated by the observatory as qcew_jobs minus qcew_private_jobs. The value is blank when either of the two is blank. The island value is the same subtraction on BLS's island figures. The BLS files also hold the federal, state and local figures, and the observatory does not publish them.
economy.qcew_gov_jobs.how_to_read: Government jobs are counted where the government office is, even if the office serves the whole island. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan holds 59,579 of the island's 192,447 government jobs in 2025 (31%). A high count in a municipality shows where public employers are located; it does not show how many residents work for government. For that, see 'Residents working for government' (economy.gov_worker_pct), from the Census survey.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, island government jobs fell from 229,541 in 2014 to 192,447 in 2025 (16.2% lower), while private jobs rose 11.5%.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra's value is blank in 2015 to 2021 (its private jobs are withheld), so 77 municipalities have a value in those years and 78 in the others. For state and local government, BLS withholds 74 to 76 of the 78 municipalities in each year from 2014 to 2021, and none from 2022.
The difference is only as exact as the two figures it comes from. Where either is withheld, the result is blank.

BLS classifies each job by the ownership of the employer. Government-owned bodies are counted here and not in the private industry variables, so, for example, public schools and government-run hospitals are not in the private education and health care variables. The data do not show how BLS classifies each public corporation.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, BLS's 2025 figures split the island's government jobs into 20,747 federal, 119,858 Commonwealth and 51,842 municipal jobs. The observatory's data file does not carry this split.
A change of operator moves jobs between government and private without any change in total jobs; the data cannot separate this effect.
An agency that reports all its staff under its headquarters site puts them all in that municipality; the observatory cannot test how each agency reports.

economy.gov_job_share_pct.plain: Out of every 100 jobs located in the municipality, how many are with government.
economy.gov_job_share_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 empleos ubicados en el municipio, cuántos son del gobierno.
economy.gov_job_share_pct.definition: Government jobs divided by all jobs located in the municipality, times 100, in the same year. Both come from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Government jobs are total jobs minus private jobs.
economy.gov_job_share_pct.method: Calculated by the observatory: round(government jobs / total jobs x 100, 2). The value is blank (not zero) when private jobs are withheld. The island value is calculated the same way from BLS's island figures.
economy.gov_job_share_pct.how_to_read: A high share means public employers provide most of the local jobs; a low share means a mostly private job base. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island share is 20.3% in 2025, and municipal shares run from 6.1% (Guaynabo) to 76.6% (Maunabo), with a middle value of 23.1%. It describes the jobs located in the municipality, not the work of the residents.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island share fell from 25.3% in 2014 to 20.3% in 2025 as government jobs fell (16.2% lower) and private jobs rose (11.5% higher); BLS's files do not show why. The middle municipal value fell from 31.1% to 23.1%.
In a small municipality a few jobs move the share by several points.
Government includes federal, Commonwealth and municipal employers, public schools and other government-owned bodies.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.
A change of operator moves jobs between government and private without any change in total jobs; the data cannot separate this effect.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra's value is blank in 2015 to 2021 because its private jobs are withheld, although its total jobs are published.
