economy.qcew_jobs.plain: How many wage-and-salary jobs exist at employers located in the municipality, averaged over the year. Jobs are counted where the work is done, not where the worker lives.
economy.qcew_jobs.plain_es: Cuántos empleos asalariados hay en patronos ubicados en el municipio, en promedio durante el año. Los empleos se cuentan donde se hace el trabajo, no donde vive la persona trabajadora.
economy.qcew_jobs.definition: Average number of jobs in the year at employers located in the municipality, private and government, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). It covers wage-and-salary jobs that fall under unemployment insurance, which the Bureau says is about 95% of jobs in the United States. The annual average is the mean of twelve monthly counts. It counts jobs, not people, and counts each job at the work site. Self-employed and informal work are not counted.
economy.qcew_jobs.method: Column annual_avg_emplvl of the BLS annual file for each municipality, ownership code 0 (all ownerships), industry code 10 (all industries). The island value is BLS's own figure for Puerto Rico (area 72000), not the sum of the 78 municipalities.
economy.qcew_jobs.how_to_read: Use it to see where the work is. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan has the most jobs: 253,816 in 2025, 27% of the island's 947,557. It is not the number of employed residents. A place that draws commuters shows more jobs than it has workers living there; to compare the two, use jobs per employed resident. The Analysis tab can show it per 1,000 residents, per square kilometer or as a share of the island total. In the dataset information window on the Analysis tab (open it with the info button beside the dataset), the 'Download all years (CSV)' button saves all years as a comma-separated values file named pr_economy_qcew_jobs.csv; blank cells are values that BLS withholds or does not report.
caveats: Covered jobs only: self-employed people, unpaid family workers, informal work and military personnel are not counted. BLS says covered employment is about 95% of jobs in the United States; the observatory does not measure the share for Puerto Rico.
Jobs are counted at the work site the employer reports. A company that reports all its workers under one site puts them all in that site's municipality.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, BLS's island figure is above the sum of the 78 municipalities by 1,681 jobs in 2014 (0.2%) and by 4,555 in 2025 (0.5%); BLS's files do not show why. All 78 municipalities have a value in every year.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island total fell from 907,001 in 2014 to 832,754 in 2020 (8.2% lower) and rose to 947,557 in 2025. A year's average mixes the months before and after any shock inside the year.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary; BLS can revise it. The observatory reads a revision only on a full refresh; these values were downloaded on 3 October 2026.

Shaded per 1,000 residents (the Analysis tab's default for counts), the map divides the jobs located in a municipality by its residents. It is not an employment rate: places with many jobs for their size score high. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan has about 770 jobs per 1,000 residents in 2025, against about 298 for Puerto Rico.

economy.jobs_per_employed_resident.plain: How many jobs are located in the municipality for each employed resident. Above 1 means more jobs than employed residents live there, so the place may draw workers from elsewhere. Below 1 means fewer jobs than employed residents. Many of those residents may work elsewhere, or in work that the jobs data do not count, such as self-employment.
economy.jobs_per_employed_resident.plain_es: Cuántos empleos hay en el municipio por cada residente con empleo. Más de 1 significa que hay más empleos que residentes con empleo, así que el lugar puede atraer personas trabajadoras de otros sitios. Menos de 1 significa que hay menos empleos que residentes con empleo. Muchas de esas personas pueden trabajar en otro lugar o en trabajos que los datos de empleos no cuentan, como el trabajo por cuenta propia.
economy.jobs_per_employed_resident.definition: Jobs located in the municipality (annual average, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)) divided by employed residents 16 and over (civilian, from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates) whose survey window ends in the same year. For 2024 the residents are those of the 2020 to 2024 window. The jobs figure is one year; the residents figure is a five-year window.
economy.jobs_per_employed_resident.method: Calculated by the observatory: round(qcew_jobs / workers_16plus, 3) for each year and place where both are above zero. workers_16plus is the ACS count of civilian employed residents 16 and over (table B24080, total), described in the entry for employed residents. The island value divides BLS's island jobs by the ACS island count of employed residents, which equals the sum of the 78 municipalities' counts.
economy.jobs_per_employed_resident.how_to_read: A value of 1 means one covered job for each employed resident. Compare a municipality with the island value, not with 1. A value well above the island value points to a place that draws workers; a low value points to a place where many residents work elsewhere. It does not say where they work. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island value is 0.82 in 2024, below 1; one reason is that the jobs count leaves out self-employed and informal work, which the resident count includes. That year, 9 of 78 municipalities are above 1: San Juan (1.91), Mayagüez (1.52), Guaynabo (1.50), Cataño (1.44), Barceloneta (1.27), Aguadilla (1.21), Ponce (1.20), Manatí (1.19), Humacao (1.05). The middle municipal value is 0.50, so a typical municipality has about one covered job for every two employed residents. The lowest is Toa Alta (0.16), and Toa Alta is the lowest in every year from 2014 to 2024.
caveats: It compares two different counts. It is consistent with commuting but does not measure it. For commuting itself, see the commute variables from the same survey.
The years do not match exactly. A QCEW year is divided by a five-year survey window that ends in that year, so the 2020 jobs dip is divided by a window that covers 2016 to 2020.

The resident count is a survey estimate with a margin of error (90% confidence). In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 margin is about 6% of the estimate in a typical municipality and 19% in Culebra. The margin is not carried into the ratio.
The jobs are counted at the employer's reporting site, so a company that reports all its workers under one site raises the ratio there.
Jobs are not people: a person with two jobs counts twice in the numerator and once in the denominator.
A low value can also reflect self-employed or informal workers, who are in the resident count but not in the jobs count.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 78 municipalities have a value in each year from 2014 to 2024, and the island count of employed residents is 1,150,831 in 2024.
economy.jobs_per_employed_resident.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value divides BLS's island jobs by the island's employed residents, which equal the sum of the 78 municipalities' counts)

economy.qcew_private_jobs.plain: How many jobs at private employers are located in the municipality, averaged over the year. Jobs at government employers are not included.
economy.qcew_private_jobs.plain_es: Cuántos empleos en patronos privados están ubicados en el municipio, en promedio durante el año. No incluye los empleos en patronos del gobierno.
economy.qcew_private_jobs.definition: Average number of jobs in the year at private-ownership employers located in the municipality, all industries, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Private ownership includes nonprofit organizations such as private schools, private hospitals and charities, as well as for-profit firms. Bodies owned by government are not included. The same coverage rules as total jobs apply: wage-and-salary jobs under unemployment insurance, counted at the work site.
economy.qcew_private_jobs.method: Column annual_avg_emplvl of the BLS annual file, ownership code 5 (private), industry code 10 (all industries). A value is blank (not zero) where BLS withholds the private figure. The island value is BLS's own figure.
economy.qcew_private_jobs.how_to_read: Private jobs are the jobs at private employers located in the municipality, not residents who work in the private sector. Subtract private jobs from total jobs to get government jobs; the observatory does this in the government jobs variable. In the 2026-10 snapshot, private jobs are 79.7% of island jobs in 2025 (755,110 of 947,557).
caveats: Includes nonprofit employers. A job at a private contractor that serves government counts as private; a job at a government-owned body counts as government.
Self-employed and informal work are not counted.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, island private jobs rose from 677,460 in 2014 to 755,110 in 2025 (11.5% higher).
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, BLS withholds Culebra's private figure from 2015 to 2021 (7 years), so Culebra's private jobs, government jobs and government share are blank (not zero) in those years, although its total jobs are published (382 to 462 jobs). The other 77 municipalities have a value in every year.

economy.qcew_wages.plain: All wages paid in the year by employers located in the municipality, in dollars of that year. It is the payroll of the jobs located there, not the income of the people who live there.
economy.qcew_wages.plain_es: Todos los salarios que pagaron en el año los patronos ubicados en el municipio, en dólares de ese año. Es la nómina de los empleos ubicados allí, no el ingreso de las personas que viven allí.
economy.qcew_wages.definition: Total annual wages paid to covered workers by employers located in the municipality, private and government, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). As BLS defines wages, they include bonuses, tips and other gratuities and the cash value of meals and lodging. They do not include the employer's contributions to Social Security, health insurance, workers' compensation or pension funds, so they are not the total cost of labor. They are in US dollars of the year paid and are not adjusted for inflation.
economy.qcew_wages.method: Column total_annual_wages of the BLS annual file, ownership code 0, industry code 10. The island value is BLS's own figure, not the sum of the 78 municipalities.
economy.qcew_wages.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan employers paid $11.23 billion in 2025, 32.5% of the island's $34.51 billion. Wages are, to within rounding, jobs times average pay, so a municipality's payroll depends on both how many jobs it has and how much they pay. It shows where the money is paid out, which is not where the people who earn it live. To compare years, tick the inflation-adjusted option on the Analysis tab; it uses the US consumer price index (CPI-U, US city average) because the observatory's sources hold no Puerto Rico index.
caveats: Dollars are not adjusted. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island total rose 40.4% from 2014 to 2025 ($24.58 billion to $34.51 billion), while the US consumer price index rose 36.0% over the same years. The US index only approximates Puerto Rico's price changes.
It does not include the income of self-employed people or informal work.
It is paid at the work site, so commuters' wages are counted in the municipality of the job.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it.

Shaded as dollars per resident (the Analysis tab's default for dollar totals), it is the payroll of local employers divided by residents. It is not the income of residents: it is high where jobs are concentrated. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's payroll is about $34,100 per resident in 2025, against about $10,800 for Puerto Rico.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, all 78 municipalities have a value in every year. BLS's island figure is above the sum of the 78 municipalities by 0.4% in 2014 and by 0.7% in 2025.

economy.qcew_method.plain: Jobs, work sites, wages and industries come from a US government count of jobs at employers who pay into the unemployment insurance system, which covers most wage-and-salary work. It counts jobs where the work is done, gives one annual average per year, and hides cells that would identify one employer.
economy.qcew_method.plain_es: Los empleos, los lugares de trabajo, los salarios y las industrias vienen de un conteo del gobierno de EE. UU. de los empleos en patronos que aportan al sistema de seguro por desempleo, que cubre la mayor parte del trabajo asalariado. Cuenta los empleos donde se hace el trabajo, da un promedio anual por año y oculta las celdas que identificarían a un solo patrono.
economy.qcew_method.definition: The Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) is built by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) from the reports that employers file for unemployment insurance. The observatory reads its annual-average files for each of the 78 municipalities and for Puerto Rico. Employment is the average of twelve monthly counts; a monthly count is the number of covered workers who worked or were paid in the pay period that includes the 12th of the month. Establishments are the average of four quarterly counts of work sites. Wages are the total paid in the year. Every figure belongs to the place of the employer's work site, not to the place where the worker lives. Each figure is split by ownership (private or government) and by industry, using the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS).
economy.qcew_method.method: (1) The observatory finds the latest year by asking BLS for the San Juan file of the next year, starting from 2024, and reads every year from 2014 to that latest year. (2) For each year it downloads one file per area: 78 municipality codes and the island code 72000. (3) From each file it keeps the all-industry rows (industry code 10) for ownership codes 0, 1, 2, 3 and 5, and, for ownership 5 only, the 19 two-digit NAICS sectors and the three-digit codes 721 and 722. (4) It reads four columns: annual_avg_estabs, annual_avg_emplvl, total_annual_wages and avg_annual_pay. If the row's disclosure_code is N, all four are left blank. (5) Publication: ownership 0 gives qcew_estabs, qcew_jobs, qcew_wages and qcew_avg_pay. Ownership 5 gives qcew_private_jobs, the 19 industry variables, accommodation_jobs (721) and food_service_jobs (722). qcew_gov_jobs is qcew_jobs minus qcew_private_jobs, and gov_job_share_pct is that difference divided by qcew_jobs times 100. tourism_jobs is sector 72 plus sector 71 (sector 72 alone where 71 is blank). industry_hhi is the Herfindahl index of the published sectors and government. The data file also holds extras.top_sector, the largest employer group of each place and year (see its entry). jobs_per_employed_resident divides qcew_jobs by the American Community Survey count of employed residents of the same year label. BLS values are published as read. The observatory rounds its own calculations: government share to 2 decimals, jobs per employed resident to 3 decimals, and the industry concentration index to a whole number.
economy.qcew_method.how_to_read: Read every QCEW figure as what employers located in the municipality reported, not as what the residents do. A blank is not a zero: it means BLS withheld the figure or publishes no row for that cell. Use the Puerto Rico value as BLS's island figure; it is not the sum of the 78 municipalities. Treat the latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) as preliminary. On the Analysis tab, a jobs count can be shown as published, per 1,000 residents, per square kilometer, as a share of the island total, as a share of the municipality's jobs, or as a location quotient. A location quotient is the industry's share of the municipality's jobs divided by its share of the island's jobs; above 1 means the industry is more concentrated here than on the island, and below 1 means less. The share and the quotient use total jobs (all employers, including government) of the same year as the divisor. The observatory downloaded every year's file on 3 October 2026. It keeps each file and reads it again only on a full refresh, so a later BLS revision, including to preliminary 2025, shows only after a refresh. The 'Data built' date in the dataset information window is the day the observatory's data file was last rebuilt, which can be later than the download. When you cite a figure, give the year, the ownership and industry row, and the retrieval date. The examples in these entries come from the 2026-10 snapshot. They use 2025 for totals (jobs, wages, pay), which have a value for every municipality, and 2024 for industry sectors, because 2025 has fewer published municipal values for sectors.
caveats: Coverage. BLS says covered employment is about 95% of jobs in the United States. The observatory does not measure the share for Puerto Rico. Not counted: proprietors and other self-employed people, unpaid family workers, informal or off-the-books work, military and National Guard members, elected officials, railroad workers covered by their own system, certain farm and domestic workers, and anyone who did not work or get paid in the pay period that includes the 12th of the month. BLS lists a few further small groups at https://www.bls.gov/cew/overview.htm .

Jobs, not people. A person with two jobs at two employers counts twice. A job at a company with several sites is counted at the site that the employer reports; if an employer reports all its workers under one site, they appear in that site's municipality. The observatory cannot test how each employer reports.

Two kinds of blank. In the BLS files, a blank industry cell is either withheld (disclosure code N) or has no row. BLS's file layout notes do not say why a row is absent, so the observatory cannot tell from the files whether a missing row means that the place has no employer in that industry. The published data file does not tell the two kinds apart. In the 2026-10 snapshot, across the 19 sectors and the 78 municipalities in 2024, 769 cells have a value, 527 are withheld and 186 have no row (of 1,482).

Blanks are most common in small municipalities and in narrow industries. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 26 municipalities with the fewest jobs in 2024 have a value in 6.5 of the 19 sectors on average; the 26 with the most jobs have 13.0. Some hidden cells look paired: in the same snapshot, 19 municipalities have the sector 72 total (hotels and restaurants) published in 2024 while both of its parts, accommodation (721) and food service (722), are blank.

The Puerto Rico value is BLS's own island figure. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it is above the sum of the 78 municipalities by 1,681 jobs (0.2%) in 2014 and by 4,555 (0.5%) in 2025. BLS's files do not give the reason. In the same snapshot, for industries the island cell is blank while municipal cells are published (construction in 2025), and it is published while almost every municipal cell is blank (mining in 2024).

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 is the latest year and is preliminary: BLS can revise it. It is also less complete: 13 of the 19 sectors have fewer municipalities with a published value in 2025 than in 2024, and five sectors (mining, utilities, construction, transportation and warehousing, information) have no island value in 2025.
Annual averages smooth changes inside a year. An event in September (such as Hurricane Maria in 2017) shows part of its effect in that year and part in the next.

The sector definitions follow NAICS, which is revised every five years. BLS classified 2014 to 2016 data with NAICS 2012, 2017 to 2021 data with NAICS 2017 and 2022 onward with NAICS 2022 (see the BLS industry classification page). The observatory does not recode earlier years to one edition, so a sector total before and after 2017 or 2022 may not be fully comparable. Check the BLS notes before reading a small change at sector level as real.

BLS also reports government jobs by level (federal, state, local, ownership codes 1, 2 and 3). The observatory downloads them but publishes only the total minus private, so government jobs cannot be split by level in this data.

values.0: All ownerships (total covered). Used for jobs, establishments, wages and average pay.
values.5: Private ownership, which includes nonprofit organizations. Used for private jobs and for every industry variable.
values.1: Federal government. The observatory downloads these rows but does not publish them in its data file.
values.2: State government (the Commonwealth in Puerto Rico). The observatory downloads these rows but does not publish them in its data file.
values.3: Local government (municipal). The observatory downloads these rows but does not publish them in its data file.
values.disclosure code N: BLS withholds the figures of the row to protect an employer's confidentiality. The observatory leaves the cell blank.

economy.qcew_method.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island figure is BLS's own and is not summed from the 78; the observatory's derived island values are calculated from BLS's island figures)
economy.qcew_method.source_detail: BLS QCEW open-data API, annual-average area files: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/<year>/a/area/<area>.csv, where <area> is the five-digit FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) code of the municipio (72001 Adjuntas, 72003 Aguada, and so on up to 72153 Yauco; 78 codes in all) or 72000 for Puerto Rico. Columns used: own_code, industry_code, disclosure_code, annual_avg_estabs, annual_avg_emplvl, total_annual_wages, avg_annual_pay. File layout: https://www.bls.gov/cew/additional-resources/open-data/ . Who is covered: https://www.bls.gov/cew/overview.htm . NAICS editions by year: https://www.bls.gov/cew/classifications/industry/home.htm .

methods.qcew_suppression.plain: The jobs data hide any cell that could reveal one employer. A blank in the observatory means the figure was withheld or no employer was listed, and it is never zero. Small municipalities and narrow industries have the most blanks.
methods.qcew_suppression.plain_es: Los datos de empleos ocultan cualquier celda que pueda revelar a un solo patrono. Un espacio en blanco en el observatorio significa que la cifra se retuvo o que no había ningún patrono registrado, y nunca equivale a cero. Los municipios pequeños y las industrias muy específicas tienen más espacios en blanco.
methods.qcew_suppression.definition: The Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) marks a withheld cell with disclosure code N. When it does, the observatory leaves all four values (work sites, jobs, total wages, average pay) blank. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the all-industry total and the private-sector total are published for every municipality in 2025. Cells for the 19 private-sector industries are often blank, and a blank can also mean the file lists no such employers. The published data file does not tell the two apart.
methods.qcew_suppression.method: qcew_area in economy_series.py reads each area-year file, keeps the all-industry rows by ownership and the sector rows for private ownership, and sets the four figures to blank when disclosure_code is N. Tourism-related jobs use code 72 of the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) alone where NAICS 71 is withheld, and are blank where 72 is. The industry concentration index is computed only where the published sectors cover at least 80% of jobs.
methods.qcew_suppression.how_to_read: Where a sector is blank for a municipality, do not add the sector figures and expect the total. The shares, location quotients and correlations built on that sector leave the municipality out. In the 2026-10 snapshot, of the 1,482 sector cells (19 sectors × 78 municipalities) in 2024, 769 have a value, 527 are withheld and 186 have no row. In 2025, the latest year, 671 have a value, 632 are withheld and 179 have no row. In 2024, 34 municipalities have no figure for accommodation and food services (NAICS code 72); in 2025 it is 39.
caveats: A blank is not zero. Treat it as unknown.
Shares of jobs by sector do not add up to 100% where cells are withheld, and sector figures add up to less than the total.

The Puerto Rico figure is the Bureau's island figure, not the sum of the 78 municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island figure for 2025 is 947,557 jobs and the 78 municipalities add up to 943,002.
Correlations that use a sector with many blanks rest on few municipalities. Check n.
methods.qcew_suppression.source_detail: Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) QCEW open-data API, annual files by area.

methods.workplace_vs_residence.plain: Some figures count where the work is done, and others count where people live. Jobs, wages and work sites are by workplace. Income, poverty, employed residents and commuting are by residence. Read the basis before comparing two figures.
methods.workplace_vs_residence.plain_es: Algunas cifras cuentan dónde se hace el trabajo y otras, dónde vive la gente. Los empleos, los salarios y los lugares de trabajo se cuentan por lugar de trabajo. El ingreso, la pobreza, las personas residentes con empleo y los viajes al trabajo se cuentan por lugar de residencia. Verifique la base antes de comparar dos cifras.
methods.workplace_vs_residence.definition: Workplace basis: a job or a work site belongs to the municipality where the employer's work site is. Residence basis: a person or household belongs to the municipality where they live, wherever they work. Other bases are named in the list of codes below.
methods.workplace_vs_residence.method: Set by each source: the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) counts by work site, the American Community Survey (ACS) and Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) count residents, and USAspending files an award by place of performance as the awarding agency reports it. The jobs-per-employed-resident ratio divides QCEW jobs (workplace) by ACS employed residents (residence).
methods.workplace_vs_residence.how_to_read: A municipality with more jobs than employed residents is a job centre that draws commuters. One with far fewer is a place where many residents work elsewhere. The ratio does not say where they work. San Juan shows the difference: in the 2026-10 snapshot it holds 253,816 jobs in 2025 (26.8% of the island's jobs) but 329,737 residents (10.4% of the island's residents), and in 2024 it has 1.91 jobs for each employed resident.
caveats: Do not use jobs per 1,000 residents as an employment rate. It counts jobs located in the municipality, not jobs held by residents.
Jobs are placed in the municipality where the employer reports each work site. The observatory does not check those reports.

QCEW counts only jobs at employers covered by unemployment insurance. Self-employed people, unpaid family workers and informal work are not counted, so jobs per employed resident compares covered jobs with all employed residents.
Jobs are not people: a person with two jobs counts twice.
A QCEW year is divided by a five-year survey window that ends in the same year, so the two are not the same period.

values.Jobs, work sites, wages, average pay (Qu: Workplace: the municipality of the employer's work site.
values.Employed residents and class of worker,: Residence: the worker's home municipality, wherever the job is.
values.Housing units and vacancy (Census counts: Neither: the location of the home, whoever lives in it.
values.Jobs per employed resident: Both: jobs at the workplace divided by workers at home.
values.Federal awards (USAspending): Place of performance as the awarding agency reports it.
values.Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEM: Applicant municipality of the project; a large part is recorded as statewide.
values.FEMA Individual Assistance (housing): The county recorded in the OpenFEMA housing assistance record.
values.Tourism places (Overture): The municipality that contains the listing's map point.

methods.workplace_vs_residence.source_detail: The definition of each series in the source's own documentation.

economy.laus_employed.plain: How many residents have a job, as a yearly average, counted where they live. The observatory calculates it from two Bureau of Labor Statistics series: the labor force (people with a job or looking for one) minus the unemployed. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: about 1.16 million for 2025.
economy.laus_employed.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes tienen empleo, como promedio anual, contadas donde viven. El observatorio lo calcula a partir de dos series del Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales (BLS): la fuerza laboral (personas con empleo o que lo buscan) menos las personas desempleadas. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: cerca de 1.16 millones en 2025.
economy.laus_employed.definition: The labor force minus the unemployed, both as yearly averages for residents 16 and over (BLS, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics). It counts people, not jobs: a resident with two jobs counts once, and a resident counts where they live, not where they work. The observatory calculates it; it is not a series BLS publishes in the observatory's files.
economy.laus_employed.method: For each municipality and year the observatory calculates: unemployed = round(labor force × unemployment rate ÷ 100); employed = round(labor force) − unemployed. The inputs are the BLS annual-average labor force (series LAUCN72xxx0000000006) and unemployment rate (LAUCN72xxx0000000003). BLS publishes the rate to one decimal, so the unemployed count, and therefore the employed count, can be off by up to 0.05% of the labor force: about 70 people where the labor force is 140,000, and less than one where it is 1,100. The Puerto Rico row uses the island series (LASST720000000000006 and LASST720000000000003, each averaged over twelve months) in the same formula.
economy.laus_employed.how_to_read: Compare it with the labor force to see how many of the people in the labor force have work. For the share without work, use the unemployment rate. On the Analysis tab a shaded layer shows it per 1,000 residents by default. That divides by the total population of all ages for the same year, not by residents 16 and over, so it is not an employment rate. To cite, name BLS and the two series it comes from and say the observatory derived it: 'Derived by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, labor force and unemployment rate, annual average 2024, retrieved [date].' For Puerto Rico, name the two island series (LASST720000000000006 and LASST720000000000003) and say that the observatory averaged their twelve monthly values.
caveats: It is not a count that BLS published. BLS also publishes its own employment series (measure 05), which the observatory does not read, so the two can differ slightly because of the rounding of the rate.

There is no value for 2020, and the observatory does not estimate one; when you choose 2020 the map shows 2019, labeled '2019 (latest at or before 2020)'. See 'How the unemployment figures are built' (economy.laus_method) for what is known.
The observatory's data hold no margin of error for these BLS series, so the Analysis tab shows none. Treat small municipalities as imprecise anyway.
The latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) is preliminary and can be revised. Check the current BLS figure before you quote it.

It is not the same as the survey count 'Employed residents 16+ (ACS)' from the American Community Survey (ACS). In the 2026-10 snapshot, for Puerto Rico the survey count is 8% higher than this one for 2010 (1,149,431 against 1,060,969). The two come from different surveys and methods, and the survey count averages five years (2006-2010); the data do not show how much each explains. For 2024 they are nearly equal (1,150,831 against 1,152,370). Do not mix the two series in one comparison.
It counts people who live in the municipality, not jobs located there. For jobs by workplace, see the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) series.
The island value is calculated from the island series, not added up from the municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 island count is 1,152,370 and the 78 municipalities add up to 1,152,649.
economy.laus_employed.source_detail: Derived by the observatory from BLS LAUS measure 06 (labor force) and measure 03 (unemployment rate), annual averages from 2010; see economy.laus_labor_force and economy.laus_unemp_rate. Definitions follow BLS (https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm).

municipalities.employment_rate_pct.plain: Out of every 100 residents aged 16 or older, how many have a civilian job. Retirees, students and others who are not looking for work are in the base, so the rate is lower than a share of the labor force.
municipalities.employment_rate_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 residentes de 16 años o más, cuántos tienen un empleo civil. Las personas jubiladas, estudiantes y otras que no buscan trabajo están en la base, así que la tasa es más baja que una proporción de la fuerza laboral.
municipalities.employment_rate_pct.definition: Employed civilians divided by the whole population aged 16 and over, times 100. From table B23025 (employment status; cells 004 and 001) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates for the latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The base is everyone aged 16 and over: employed civilians, unemployed civilians, members of the armed forces (these three make up the labor force) and people not in the labor force.
municipalities.employment_rate_pct.method: B23025 cell 004 ('Employed', civilian) divided by cell 001 (total population 16 and over), times 100, rounded to one decimal (file acsdt5y2024-b23025.dat in the 2026-10 snapshot).
municipalities.employment_rate_pct.how_to_read: A low value can reflect a large share of retirees, students or people who are not looking for work, as well as few jobs. It is not the unemployment rate.
caveats: It counts residents where they live. It does not count jobs located in the municipality; for jobs by workplace see 'Jobs (all employers)' (Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, QCEW).
It is not the unemployment rate. For that, see 'Unemployment rate (BLS)' (Local Area Unemployment Statistics, LAUS), which is measured differently.

A survey estimate. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), the Housing page series shows a 90% margin of error from ±0.7 points (San Juan) to ±5.9 points (Culebra and Vieques). The municipality file (municipalities.json) carries the estimate only, with no margin.
municipalities.employment_rate_pct.source_detail: ACS 5-year 2020-2024, table B23025 (employment status for the population 16 years and over), cell 004 divided by cell 001

view.label: Map, Rankings tab: download the municipality table (CSV)
Housing page: full data for every year, with trend chart and CSV
Housing page: municipality profile

housing.employment_rate_pct.plain: Out of every 100 residents aged 16 or older, how many had a civilian job. It counts retirees, students and everyone else who is not working, so it is lower than the share of people in the labor force. Puerto Rico: 41.3% in 2020-2024.
housing.employment_rate_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 residentes de 16 años o más, cuántos tenían un empleo civil. Incluye a las personas jubiladas, estudiantes y todas las demás que no trabajan, por lo que es más bajo que la proporción de personas en la fuerza laboral. Puerto Rico: 41.3% en 2020-2024.
housing.employment_rate_pct.definition: Employed civilians (American Community Survey, ACS, table B23025, cell 4) divided by all residents 16 and over (B23025, cell 1), times 100: the employment-to-population ratio. A person is employed if they worked for pay or profit, or had a job and were away, in the week before answering the survey. Members of the armed forces are in the base but not in the numerator.
housing.employment_rate_pct.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 4 by cell 1. The observatory treats table B23025 as unavailable for the 2006-2010 window, so the series starts with 2007-2011 (labeled 2011). The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator.
housing.employment_rate_pct.how_to_read: A value of 41 means that 41 of every 100 residents aged 16 or older had a civilian job. The base includes retirees, students and everyone else who is not in the labor force, so the rate reflects the age mix as well as the number of jobs. It is not the share of job seekers who found work; for that, see the unemployment rate. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
The base includes people who are not in the labor force. In Puerto Rico in 2020-2024, 1,495,476 of 2,788,407 residents aged 16 and over (54%) were outside the labor force.
It counts where people live, not where jobs are. For jobs by workplace, see the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) jobs series.

Estimates for small municipalities are imprecise. The municipality profile warns for municipalities with fewer than 25,000 residents. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.
The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 50% of barrios and 13% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
housing.employment_rate_pct.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts
housing.employment_rate_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B23025 (Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over), cells 001 and 004; windows 2007-2011 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b23025.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).

economy.laus_method.plain: The observatory's unemployment figures are yearly averages of Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) estimates for the residents of each municipality and for Puerto Rico; the observatory calculates the employed and unemployed counts itself. There is no 2020 value.
economy.laus_method.plain_es: Las cifras de desempleo del observatorio son promedios anuales de los estimados del BLS (Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales) para las personas residentes de cada municipio y de Puerto Rico; el observatorio calcula por su cuenta los conteos de personas con empleo y desempleadas. No hay valor para 2020.
economy.laus_method.definition: Four variables come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) program: the unemployment rate and the labor force are BLS series; the employed and unemployed counts are calculated by the observatory from those two. All four are yearly averages for residents, by where they live. For municipalities they are Bureau estimates built from local administrative and survey data and controlled to state totals, not direct counts.
economy.laus_method.method: 1. Series. For each municipality: LAUCN72xxx0000000003 (measure 03, unemployment rate) and LAUCN72xxx0000000006 (measure 06, labor force), where 72xxx is the municipality's five-digit code (San Juan is 72127). For Puerto Rico: LASST720000000000003 and LASST720000000000006. The observatory asks the BLS public data interface (API, version 1, no key) with the annual-average option for every year from 2010 to the last full calendar year. 2. Annual averages. For municipalities the observatory stores BLS's own annual average (period M13, the code BLS uses for the annual average): the rate to one decimal, the labor force as a whole number. For Puerto Rico the BLS data hold no published annual average, so the observatory takes the simple mean of the twelve monthly values; the island rate therefore carries more decimals and the island labor force is rounded to a whole person. 3. Derived counts. Unemployed = round(labor force × rate ÷ 100). Employed = round(labor force) − unemployed. Because BLS publishes the rate to one decimal, a derived count can be off by up to 0.05% of the labor force.
economy.laus_method.how_to_read: Use the rate to compare places and years; use the counts to show how many people are affected. For small municipalities, read the trend over several years, not one year. On the Analysis tab, when the chosen year has no value, the map shows the latest earlier year and labels it (for 2020, '2019 (latest at or before 2020)'). The workbench trend chart lists only the years that have data. In the inspector, the small trend line spaces years by the calendar. The caption under it gives the length of the trend in years, the number of values when years are missing, and the first and last year: in the 2026-10 snapshot, an unemployment series reads '16 yrs, 15 values · 2010–25'. The info (i) button beside a dataset opens its definition and sources, links to its entry in this dictionary and offers a CSV of every year. To cite BLS data, give the series ID, the year, the program and the retrieval date: 'US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, series LAUCN721270000000003 (San Juan Municipio, Puerto Rico), annual average 2024, retrieved [date].' For Puerto Rico, cite the average of the twelve monthly values of series LASST720000000000003 and say that Foundation for Puerto Rico's PR Data Observatory calculated it. For the employed and unemployed counts, say that the observatory derived them.
caveats: The estimates are not a head count and not a separate survey of each municipality. For municipalities they are a Bureau estimate built from local administrative and survey data and controlled to state totals. BLS's county-method page describes how it builds county estimates (from employment and claims data, controlled to state totals) but does not say how Puerto Rico's municipio estimates are made. BLS's technical note says Puerto Rico's island estimates come from a monthly household survey similar to the Current Population Survey.

Small municipalities swing. In the 2026-10 snapshot, across pairs of consecutive years (2019 to 2021 is left out), the median size of the change in a municipality's rate, ignoring direction and using the labor force of the later year, is 1.9 points where the labor force is under 3,000 (46 year pairs, five municipalities), 1.1 points between 3,000 and 20,000 and 0.7 points over 20,000 (141 year pairs, 11 municipalities).
The observatory's data hold no margin of error for these BLS series, so the Analysis tab shows none. Treat small municipalities as imprecise anyway.
The latest year is preliminary and can be revised (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot). Check the current BLS figure before you quote it.

No 2020 value. For 2020 the BLS data held an annual-average row with no number for any municipality. The observatory does not fall back to monthly values when that row is present, so it cannot say whether BLS published monthly values for municipalities in 2020. For Puerto Rico the BLS data had no complete set of twelve monthly values. So there is no 2020 value, and the observatory does not estimate one. The data do not say why.

The island row is the island series, not the sum of the 78 municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, in every year with data the island labor force is within 0.4% of the municipal sum and the island unemployed count within 0.9%.
The series are for residents. They do not show where the jobs are; for that, see the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) series.

In BLS series codes, LAUCN is the county series that is not seasonally adjusted and LASST is the state series that is seasonally adjusted, so the island row and the municipal rows are built differently.

Not comparable with the survey rates 'Unemployment rate' (housing.unemployment_rate_pct) and 'Employment rate (16 and over)' (housing.employment_rate_pct). They come from the American Community Survey (ACS) and appear on the Analysis tab, as 'Unemployment rate (ACS survey)' and 'Employment rate, residents 16+ (ACS)', and on the Housing page.
economy.laus_method.source_detail: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), annual averages from 2010, through the BLS public data interface (API) at https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/. Estimation method: https://www.bls.gov/lau/laumthd.htm. BLS technical note: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/laus.tn.htm. Definitions: https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm. Series codes: https://www.bls.gov/help/hlpforma.htm.

economy.laus_labor_force.plain: How many residents 16 and over have a job or are looking for one, as a yearly average from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It counts people where they live. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: about 1.23 million for 2025.
economy.laus_labor_force.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes de 16 años o más tienen empleo o lo están buscando, como promedio anual del Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales (BLS). Cuenta a las personas donde viven. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: cerca de 1.23 millones en 2025.
economy.laus_labor_force.definition: The yearly average number of residents 16 and over who are employed or unemployed (measure 06, labor force, of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, BLS, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, LAUS). Residents with no job who are not looking, such as retirees, students and people who stopped looking, are not counted. The count is by place of residence: a person who lives in Caguas and works in San Juan is counted in Caguas. BLS counts civilians who do not live in an institution such as a prison or nursing home. Like the unemployment rate, it is a Bureau estimate and not a direct count.
economy.laus_labor_force.method: The observatory asks the BLS public data interface (API) for one series per municipality, LAUCN72xxx0000000006, where 72xxx is the municipality's five-digit code and the last two digits, 06, mean labor force. It stores BLS's annual average (period M13, the code BLS uses for the annual average) as published, a whole number. For Puerto Rico it uses the series LASST720000000000006. The BLS data hold no published annual average for that series, so the observatory takes the mean of its twelve monthly levels and rounds it to a whole person. The island value is not computed from the 78 municipalities.
economy.laus_labor_force.how_to_read: It is the base of the unemployment rate (rate = unemployed ÷ labor force). As a count it mostly shows how big a place is. On the Analysis tab a shaded layer shows it per 1,000 residents by default. That divides by the total population of all ages for the same year, not by residents 16 and over, so it is not a participation, employment or unemployment rate; for the unemployment rate use the rate layer. As symbols, the circle area is proportional to the count. It is not the number of jobs and not the number of employed residents. To compare places, use the unemployment rate. To cite a municipality: 'US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, series LAUCN721270000000006 (San Juan Municipio, Puerto Rico), annual average 2024, retrieved [date].' The five digits after LAUCN are the municipality's Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) code, shown as GEOID in the CSV from the info (i) button. For Puerto Rico the observatory uses series LASST720000000000006 and averages its twelve monthly values itself; BLS does not supply that annual average in the observatory's data. Cite the island value as: 'Average of the twelve monthly values of US Bureau of Labor Statistics series LASST720000000000006 (Puerto Rico), annual average 2024, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, retrieved [date].' If you took any number from the observatory, also cite Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory.
caveats: There is no value for 2020, and the observatory does not estimate one; when you choose 2020 the map shows 2019, labeled '2019 (latest at or before 2020)'. See 'How the unemployment figures are built' (economy.laus_method) for what is known.

The smallest municipalities have very small labor forces. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra has 1,109 and Maricao 1,620 people in the labor force for 2025, and three municipalities have fewer than 3,000. Their yearly figures are noisy.
The observatory's data hold no margin of error for these BLS series, so the Analysis tab shows none. Treat small municipalities as imprecise anyway.
The latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) is preliminary and can be revised. Check the current BLS figure before you quote it.

The Puerto Rico row is a separate BLS series, not the sum of the 78 municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot the two are close but not equal: in every year with data the island labor force is within 0.4% of the municipal sum and the island unemployed count within 0.9%.

It is a different count from the survey series 'Employed residents 16+ (ACS)' (from the American Community Survey, ACS), which covers only people with a job and pools five years of responses. In the 2026-10 snapshot, for Puerto Rico that survey count is 1.08 times the observatory's BLS-based employed count (labor force minus unemployed) for 2010 and 1.00 times for 2024, so the two series cannot be spliced.
economy.laus_labor_force.source_detail: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), annual averages from 2010, through the BLS public data interface (API) at https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/. Series LAUCN72xxx0000000006 (municipalities) and LASST720000000000006 (Puerto Rico), measure 06 (labor force). Definitions follow BLS (https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm).

economy.laus_unemployed.plain: How many residents have no job and are looking for one, as a yearly average, counted where they live. The observatory calculates it as the labor force times the unemployment rate. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: about 68,800 for 2025.
economy.laus_unemployed.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes no tienen empleo y lo están buscando, como promedio anual, contadas donde viven. El observatorio lo calcula como la fuerza laboral multiplicada por la tasa de desempleo. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: cerca de 68,800 en 2025.
economy.laus_unemployed.definition: The labor force multiplied by the unemployment rate, as yearly averages for residents 16 and over (US Bureau of Labor Statistics, BLS, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, LAUS). A resident is unemployed if they have no job, looked for work in the last four weeks and are available to start; people on temporary layoff who expect to be called back are also counted as unemployed. People who stopped looking are not counted. The observatory calculates it; it is not a series BLS publishes in the observatory's files.
economy.laus_unemployed.method: For each municipality and year the observatory calculates: unemployed = round(labor force × unemployment rate ÷ 100). The inputs are the BLS annual-average labor force (series LAUCN72xxx0000000006) and unemployment rate (LAUCN72xxx0000000003). BLS publishes the rate to one decimal, so the result can be off by up to 0.05% of the labor force: about 70 people where the labor force is 140,000, and less than one where it is 1,100. The Puerto Rico row uses the island series (LASST720000000000006 and LASST720000000000003, each averaged over twelve months) in the same formula.
economy.laus_unemployed.how_to_read: Use it to see how many people are affected; use the unemployment rate to compare places of different size. On the Analysis tab a shaded layer shows it per 1,000 residents by default. That divides by the total population of all ages for the same year, not by residents 16 and over, so it is not the unemployment rate; for the rate use the rate layer. As symbols, circle area is proportional to the count. To cite, name BLS and the two series it comes from and say the observatory derived it: 'Derived by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, labor force and unemployment rate, annual average 2024, retrieved [date].' For Puerto Rico, name the two island series (LASST720000000000006 and LASST720000000000003) and say that the observatory averaged their twelve monthly values.
caveats: It is not a count that BLS published. BLS also publishes its own unemployment series (measure 04), which the observatory does not read, so the two can differ slightly because of the rounding of the rate.

There is no value for 2020, and the observatory does not estimate one; when you choose 2020 the map shows 2019, labeled '2019 (latest at or before 2020)'. See 'How the unemployment figures are built' (economy.laus_method) for what is known.
The observatory's data hold no margin of error for these BLS series, so the Analysis tab shows none. Treat small municipalities as imprecise anyway.
The latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) is preliminary and can be revised. Check the current BLS figure before you quote it.
A small municipality has few unemployed people, and the yearly estimate is noisy: in the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra has 18 and Maricao 429 for 2025.
The island value is calculated from the island series, not added up from the municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2021 island count is 93,700 and the 78 municipalities add up to 92,920.
It counts residents, not jobs. For jobs by workplace, see the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) series.
economy.laus_unemployed.source_detail: Derived by the observatory from BLS LAUS measure 06 (labor force) and measure 03 (unemployment rate), annual averages from 2010; see economy.laus_labor_force and economy.laus_unemp_rate. Definitions follow BLS (https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm).

housing.unemployment_rate_pct.plain: Out of every 100 civilians who have a job or are looking for one, how many are looking and have no job. This is the survey estimate for a five-year window, not the monthly rate the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes. Puerto Rico: 10.7% in 2020-2024.
housing.unemployment_rate_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas civiles que tienen empleo o lo están buscando, cuántas lo buscan y no tienen empleo. Es el estimado de la encuesta para una ventana de cinco años, no la tasa mensual que publica el BLS (Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales). Puerto Rico: 10.7% en 2020-2024.
housing.unemployment_rate_pct.definition: Unemployed civilians (American Community Survey, ACS, table B23025, cell 5) divided by the civilian labor force (B23025, cell 3: employed plus unemployed), times 100. A person is unemployed if they had no job in the week before answering the survey, looked for work in the previous four weeks and were available to start.
housing.unemployment_rate_pct.method: The observatory reads the table for every window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2020 and the table-based summary files for 2021-2024, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 5 by cell 3. The observatory treats table B23025 as unavailable for the 2006-2010 window, so the series starts with 2007-2011 (labeled 2011). The margin of error of the share is computed by the observatory from the published margins of its parts, with the Census Bureau's formulas for sums (margins added in quadrature) and for a proportion whose numerator is part of the denominator.
housing.unemployment_rate_pct.how_to_read: A value of 10 means that 10 of every 100 people in the labor force were out of work and looking. People who gave up looking are not counted. Use the Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS) series from the BLS for the latest year; use this series to compare municipalities within one window. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error. At 90% confidence, the true value probably lies within that distance of the estimate.
caveats: Not comparable with the BLS series. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the BLS annual average for Puerto Rico is 5.6% for 2024 and between 5.6% and 8.0% for 2021 to 2024, while this survey shows 10.7% for the 2020-2024 window. The two sources use different surveys and methods, and the survey figure blends five years, so the numbers differ.

Noisy in small municipalities. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 201 of the 1,092 municipality estimates (78 municipalities in 14 windows, 2011 to 2024; about 1 in 5) have a margin of error larger than 30% of the estimate. The three estimates of 0.0 are not among the 201. The Full data dialog shows in italics any nonzero value whose margin of error is more than 30% of the estimate. Zero values and values with no published margin are not italicized, so an unmarked value is not proof of precision.
A value of 0.0 is a sample result, not proof that nobody is unemployed. In 2020-2024 Culebra shows 0.0% (± 2.1 points) and Maricao 0.0% (± 1.1 points).

Neighboring windows share four of their five years. To judge change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024 (labeled 2014, 2019 and 2024). See the entry on American Community Survey 5-year windows.
The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island-level estimate, not an average of the 78 municipalities.

Also published for barrios and census tracts (acs_barrio.json and acs_tract.json), each value with its margin of error where the Census Bureau gives one. Below the municipality the figure is rough. In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the CSV by area marks such values as less reliable; no map or table draws areas below the municipality yet) for 96% of barrios and more than 99% of census tracts that have a value. See methods.small_area_estimates.
housing.unemployment_rate_pct.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts
housing.unemployment_rate_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B23025 (Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over), cells 003 and 005; windows 2007-2011 to 2020-2024. Files, under https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/: for windows labeled 2021 to 2024, a table-based file such as 2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b23025.dat; for windows labeled 2010 to 2020, the per-sequence files in {year}/data/5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico/All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups/, where {year} is the last year of the window. Definitions follow the Census Bureau's ACS Subject Definitions (2024 edition: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf; each earlier year has its own edition).

economy.laus_unemp_rate.plain: Out of every 100 residents aged 16 and over who have a job or are looking for one, how many are looking for work and have none. It is a yearly average that the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) estimates for each municipality, not a head count. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 5.6% for 2025.
economy.laus_unemp_rate.plain_es: De cada 100 personas residentes de 16 años o más que tienen empleo o lo están buscando, cuántas buscan trabajo y no lo tienen. Es un promedio anual que el BLS (Negociado de Estadísticas Laborales) estima para cada municipio, no un conteo de personas. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 5.6% en 2025.
economy.laus_unemp_rate.definition: The number of unemployed residents divided by the labor force, times 100, as a yearly average from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) program called Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS). The labor force is the civilian residents 16 and over who do not live in an institution such as a prison or nursing home and who have a job or are looking for one. A resident is unemployed if they have no job, looked for work in the last four weeks and are available to start; people on temporary layoff who expect to be called back are also counted as unemployed. People who stopped looking are in neither group. The rate is for where people live, not where jobs are. For municipalities it is a Bureau estimate built from local administrative and survey data and controlled to state totals. It is not a direct count and not a separate survey of each municipality. BLS's county-method page describes how it builds county estimates but does not say how Puerto Rico's municipio estimates are made, and BLS's technical note says Puerto Rico's island estimates come from a monthly household survey similar to the Current Population Survey.
economy.laus_unemp_rate.method: The observatory asks the BLS public data interface (API) for one series per municipality, LAUCN72xxx0000000003, where 72xxx is the municipality's five-digit code (San Juan is 72127) and the last two digits, 03, mean unemployment rate. It requests the annual-average option and stores BLS's annual average (period M13, the code BLS uses for the annual average) as published, to one decimal. For Puerto Rico it uses the series LASST720000000000003. The BLS data hold no published annual average for that series, so the observatory takes the simple mean of its twelve monthly rates; this is why the island values carry more decimals and the Analysis tab shows them rounded to one. The 78 municipal values are never averaged to get the island value.
economy.laus_unemp_rate.how_to_read: A value of 5.6 means that 5.6 of every 100 people in the labor force were out of work and looking. Use it to follow one place over time or to compare larger municipalities in one year. Do not read small differences between small municipalities as real. To cite a municipality: 'US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, series LAUCN721270000000003 (San Juan Municipio, Puerto Rico), annual average 2024, retrieved [date].' The five digits after LAUCN are the municipality's Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) code (72127 for San Juan), shown as GEOID in the CSV from the info (i) button. Give the date you retrieved the data; the info box shows the date the observatory built its file. For Puerto Rico the observatory uses series LASST720000000000003 and averages its twelve monthly values itself; BLS does not supply that annual average in the observatory's data. Cite the island value as: 'Average of the twelve monthly values of US Bureau of Labor Statistics series LASST720000000000003 (Puerto Rico), annual average 2024, calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, retrieved [date].' If you took any number from the observatory, also cite Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory.
caveats: There is no value for 2020, and the observatory does not estimate one; when you choose 2020 the map shows 2019, labeled '2019 (latest at or before 2020)'. See 'How the unemployment figures are built' (economy.laus_method) for what is known.

Small municipalities swing from year to year: in the 2026-10 snapshot, Maricao (labor force 1,620 in 2025) shows 27.8% in 2017, 15.3% in 2024 and 26.5% in 2025. For how large the typical swing is, see 'How the unemployment figures are built' (economy.laus_method).
The observatory's data hold no margin of error for these BLS series, so the Analysis tab shows none. Treat small municipalities as imprecise anyway.

The latest year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot) is preliminary and can be revised. Check the current BLS figure before you quote it. In the 2026-10 snapshot, five municipalities rise by 4 points or more from 2024 to 2025: Maricao (15.3% to 26.5%), Adjuntas (7.7% to 14.7%), Guánica (11.7% to 17.3%), Las Marías (10.4% to 15.1%) and Quebradillas (5.4% to 9.6%). The data do not explain these jumps.
It counts residents, not jobs. A person who lives in Caguas and works in San Juan counts in Caguas. For jobs by workplace, see the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) series.

Not comparable with the survey rate 'Unemployment rate' (housing.unemployment_rate_pct), which the Analysis tab labels 'Unemployment rate (ACS survey)' and the Housing page also shows. In the 2026-10 snapshot, that American Community Survey (ACS) rate for Puerto Rico is 10.7% for 2020-2024, while the BLS annual averages are 8.0% (2021), 6.0% (2022), 5.9% (2023) and 5.6% (2024). The two use different sources and methods, and the data do not explain the gap.

The island rate comes from a different BLS series than the municipal rates. In BLS series codes, LAUCN is the county series that is not seasonally adjusted and LASST is the state series that is seasonally adjusted (https://www.bls.gov/help/hlpforma.htm). The island rate is therefore not exactly the labor-force-weighted average of the municipal rates: in the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2021 island rate is 8.0%, against 7.9% from the municipal counts.

Different periods side by side. With Year set to Latest, each layer on the Analysis tab uses its own latest period. In the 2026-10 snapshot, in the view 'Poverty and unemployment' the poverty rate is the 2020-2024 survey average and the unemployment rate is the 2025 annual average. Check the year chip in the legend.
economy.laus_unemp_rate.source_detail: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), annual averages from 2010, through the BLS public data interface (API) at https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/. Series LAUCN72xxx0000000003 (municipalities) and LASST720000000000003 (Puerto Rico), measure 03 (unemployment rate). Definitions follow BLS (https://www.bls.gov/cps/definitions.htm). Method notes: https://www.bls.gov/lau/laumthd.htm (county method) and https://www.bls.gov/news.release/laus.tn.htm (technical note). Read BLS's own pages before you describe the method in your own work.

labor_sex.lfpr_men.plain: Out of every 100 men aged 16 and over who live in the area, how many are working or looking for work, as the survey estimates it.
labor_sex.lfpr_men.plain_es: De cada 100 hombres de 16 años o más que viven en el área, cuántos trabajan o buscan trabajo, según el estimado de la encuesta.
labor_sex.lfpr_men.definition: Men 16 and over in the labor force (employed or unemployed, civilian or in the Armed Forces) divided by all men 16 and over, in percent (ACS B23001, as in table S2301).
labor_sex.lfpr_men.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). The rate is the men's labor force over the men's population, with the Census Bureau's margin formula for a proportion.
labor_sex.lfpr_men.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 51.4% (± 0.3 points) of the men 16 and over of Puerto Rico were in the labor force (51.3% in 2010-2014, 49.8% in 2015-2019). Among the municipios it runs from 36.0% (± 4.1) in Ciales to 63.1% (± 2.5) in Gurabo. Read it beside the women's rate (labor_sex.lfpr_women); their difference is labor_sex.lfpr_gap.
caveats: A survey estimate, not a count: every value has a 90% margin of error (the Analysis tab shows it); two areas differ significantly only when the difference is larger than its own margin.
Small municipios have wide margins: in 2020-2024 Culebra's men's rate is 53.8% ± 11.9 points and Vieques's 49.9% ± 10.8.

The three windows share no year, so they can be compared with each other; do not set them beside the ACS 5-year windows that overlap them (2016-2020 to 2019-2023, for example), which share years with them.
Counts the Armed Forces in the labor force, as table S2301 does.
labor_sex.lfpr_men.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the Census Bureau's own island row)
labor_sex.lfpr_men.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B23001, cells 001-173 (males from 003, females from 089), vintages 2014 and 2019 (per-sequence files, 5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico) and 2024 (table-based file acsdt5y2024-b23001.dat), https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/

labor_sex.lfpr_women.plain: Out of every 100 women aged 16 and over who live in the area, how many are working or looking for work, as the survey estimates it.
labor_sex.lfpr_women.plain_es: De cada 100 mujeres de 16 años o más que viven en el área, cuántas trabajan o buscan trabajo, según el estimado de la encuesta.
labor_sex.lfpr_women.definition: Women 16 and over in the labor force (employed, or unemployed: without work, looking for it and available), civilian or in the Armed Forces, divided by all women 16 and over, in percent (ACS B23001). This is the definition of ACS table S2301, which counts the Armed Forces in the labor force.
labor_sex.lfpr_women.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). The rate is the women's labor force over the women's population, both summed over the seven age groups, and its margin follows the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion (ACS General Handbook, chapter 8). The value for a group of municipios is pooled: summed counts over summed counts, never an average of the municipio rates.
labor_sex.lfpr_women.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 41.9% (± 0.3 points) of the women 16 and over of Puerto Rico were in the labor force, against 51.4% (± 0.3) of the men; the women's rate was 40.4% in 2010-2014 and 39.8% in 2015-2019. Among the municipios it runs from 26.7% (± 5.7) in Maricao to 51.8% (± 2.3) in Trujillo Alto, leaving aside Culebra (64.0% ± 10.4), whose margin is too wide to rank. The rate counts every woman 16 and over, retired women included, so a municipio with an older population has a lower rate for that reason alone; the 25-to-54 rate (labor_sex.lfpr_women_prime) and the age-adjusted rate of the Knowledge Area page take that out.
caveats: A survey estimate, not a count: every value has a 90% margin of error (the Analysis tab shows it); two areas differ significantly only when the difference is larger than its own margin.
Small municipios have wide margins: in 2020-2024 Culebra's women's rate is 64.0% ± 10.4 points and Vieques's 38.6% ± 10.3, so neither can be ranked against most others.

The three windows share no year, so they can be compared with each other; do not set them beside the ACS 5-year windows that overlap them (2016-2020 to 2019-2023, for example), which share years with them.
Counts the Armed Forces in the labor force, as table S2301 does; the Bureau of Labor Statistics' rate counts the civilian population only, so the two differ slightly.
labor_sex.lfpr_women.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (the island value is the Census Bureau's own island row)
labor_sex.lfpr_women.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B23001, cells 001-173 (males from 003, females from 089), vintages 2014 and 2019 (per-sequence files, 5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico) and 2024 (table-based file acsdt5y2024-b23001.dat), https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/

labor_sex.lfpr_women_prime.plain: Out of every 100 women aged 25 to 54 in the area, how many are working or looking for work. Leaving out the ages when many study or have retired makes areas easier to compare.
labor_sex.lfpr_women_prime.plain_es: De cada 100 mujeres de 25 a 54 años del área, cuántas trabajan o buscan trabajo. Dejar fuera las edades en que muchas estudian o están jubiladas facilita comparar áreas.
labor_sex.lfpr_women_prime.definition: Women 25 to 54 (the prime working ages) in the labor force, civilian or Armed Forces, divided by all women 25 to 54, in percent (ACS B23001, age groups 25-34, 35-44 and 45-54).
labor_sex.lfpr_women_prime.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). The rate adds the female 25-34, 35-44 and 45-54 groups (cells 110 to 137) and divides their labor force by their population, with the Census Bureau's margin formula for a proportion.
labor_sex.lfpr_women_prime.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 69.9% (± 0.5 points) of the women 25 to 54 of Puerto Rico were in the labor force, up from 63.0% in 2010-2014 and 64.6% in 2015-2019: a rise much larger than that of the 16-and-over rate, which the growing number of older women holds down. Among the municipios it runs from 52.2% (± 11.1) in Maricao to 81.0% (± 3.6) in Trujillo Alto. The margins are wider than those of the 16-and-over rate: 51 of the 78 municipios have a margin above 5 points.
caveats: A survey estimate, not a count: every value has a 90% margin of error (the Analysis tab shows it); two areas differ significantly only when the difference is larger than its own margin.

labor_sex.lfpr_gap.plain: How many percentage points higher the men's labor force participation rate is than the women's in the area; a negative value means the women's rate is higher.
labor_sex.lfpr_gap.plain_es: Cuántos puntos porcentuales más alta es la tasa de participación en la fuerza laboral de los hombres que la de las mujeres en el área; un valor negativo indica que la de las mujeres es más alta.
labor_sex.lfpr_gap.definition: The labor force participation rate of men 16 and over minus that of women 16 and over, in percentage points (ACS B23001). Its margin is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of the two rates.
labor_sex.lfpr_gap.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). The two rates are worked out as in labor_sex.lfpr_men and labor_sex.lfpr_women and subtracted; the margin of the difference treats the two rates as independent, as the Census Bureau's formula for a difference does.
labor_sex.lfpr_gap.how_to_read: In 2020-2024 the men's rate in Puerto Rico was 9.5 points (± 0.4) above the women's, against 10.8 points in 2010-2014 and 10.1 in 2015-2019. In 67 of the 78 municipios the gap is larger than its margin, so men's participation is significantly higher there. Only Culebra shows women ahead (-10.3 points), but its margin of ± 15.8 points means the survey cannot tell; the largest gaps are in Barranquitas and Comerío (18.5 points).
caveats: A survey estimate, not a count: every value has a 90% margin of error (the Analysis tab shows it); two areas differ significantly only when the difference is larger than its own margin.
Small municipios have wide margins: in 2020-2024 Culebra's gap is -10.3 ± 15.8 points and Vieques's 11.2 ± 14.9.

The three windows share no year, so they can be compared with each other; do not set them beside the ACS 5-year windows that overlap them (2016-2020 to 2019-2023, for example), which share years with them.
A gap can narrow because women's participation rises or because men's falls: read it with the two rates.
