labor_sex.unemp_women.plain: Out of every 100 women in the civilian labor force of the area, how many have no job and are looking for one, as the survey estimates it.
labor_sex.unemp_women.plain_es: De cada 100 mujeres en la fuerza laboral civil del área, cuántas no tienen empleo y lo buscan, según el estimado de la encuesta.
labor_sex.unemp_women.definition: Unemployed women 16 and over (without work, looking for it and available) divided by women 16 and over in the civilian labor force, in percent (ACS B23001). The Armed Forces are left out of the denominator, as in table S2301.
labor_sex.unemp_women.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). The rate is the women's unemployed over the women's civilian labor force, with the Census Bureau's margin formula for a proportion.
labor_sex.unemp_women.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 10.8% (± 0.3 points) of the women in Puerto Rico's civilian labor force were unemployed, down from 18.2% in 2010-2014 and 16.2% in 2015-2019. Among the municipios the margins are wide (22 of 78 above 5 points): Guánica's 25.4% has a margin of ± 8.8 and Maricao's 0.0% one of ± 9.4, so neither is a firm extreme. For the yearly unemployment rate of all residents use the Bureau of Labor Statistics series (economy.laus_unemp_rate), a model estimate.
caveats: A survey estimate, not a count: every value has a 90% margin of error (the Analysis tab shows it); two areas differ significantly only when the difference is larger than its own margin.
Small municipios have wide margins: in 2020-2024 Culebra's rate is 0.0% ± 13.9 points and Vieques's 10.9% ± 10.1.

The three windows share no year, so they can be compared with each other; do not set them beside the ACS 5-year windows that overlap them (2016-2020 to 2019-2023, for example), which share years with them.
A five-year average of survey answers: it does not show the year-to-year swings of the Bureau of Labor Statistics' yearly rate, and the two are not the same measure.

labor_sex.women_labor.plain: The survey counts behind the Women in the labor force page: for Puerto Rico and each municipio, how many women and men of each age group live there, are in the labor force and are unemployed, with margins of error, so the rate of any group of municipios can be worked out.
labor_sex.women_labor.plain_es: Los conteos de la encuesta detrás de la página Las mujeres en la fuerza laboral: para Puerto Rico y cada municipio, cuántas mujeres y hombres de cada grupo de edad viven allí, están en la fuerza laboral y están desempleados, con márgenes de error, para poder calcular la tasa de cualquier grupo de municipios.
labor_sex.women_labor.definition: women_labor.json holds, under areas.<window> (2014, 2019 and 2024, for 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024) and keyed by GEOID (72 for Puerto Rico and the 78 municipios), for each sex (m, f) and the seven age groups of ages (16-19 to 65 and over), four counts in the order of cells: pop (population), lf (labor force, civilian and Armed Forces), clf (civilian labor force) and une (unemployed), each as [estimate, 90% margin]; kids: the women 20 to 64 and those in the labor force by age of own children (u6: with a child under 6; 617: children 6 to 17 only; none), from B23003; sample: the survey's unweighted people and housing units (2020-2024 only, B98003 and B98001). groups lists the 15 municipios of the Eastern Region of FPR's Eastern Region Strategic Vision (ersv) and the seven tourism regions; names gives each municipio's name. analysis.ersv holds, for each window, the region's measures (pooled rates with margins), those of the rest of the island and of Puerto Rico, the differences with the rest of the island and whether each is significant at 90%, the gender gaps, the age-adjusted rate with its Kitagawa split and the unweighted mean of the 15 municipio rates, and the change from 2010-2014 to 2020-2024.
labor_sex.women_labor.method: women_labor.py reads ACS 5-year table B23001 (Sex by Age by Employment Status for the Population 16 Years and Over) for each window: the per-sequence summary files for 2010-2014 and 2015-2019 and the table-based files for 2020-2024. For each sex it adds the cells of seven age groups (16-19, 20-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65 and over) into four counts: population, labor force (civilian and Armed Forces), civilian labor force and unemployed. The margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins of its cells (a cell the Census Bureau controls to its own estimate has no printed margin and adds none). B23003 (Presence of Own Children Under 18 Years by Age of Own Children by Employment Status for Females 20 to 64 Years) is read the same way. A group's counts are the sums of its municipios' counts (margins added in quadrature) and its rates are pooled: summed labor force over summed population, never an average of rates. A region is compared with the rest of the island, not with the island total that contains it. A difference is significant when it is larger than its own 90% margin. The age-adjusted rate applies the region's rate in each age group to the age mix of the women 16 and over in the rest of the island (direct standardization); the gap with the rest of the island splits into a part due to the age mix and a part due to the rates within each age group (Kitagawa, 1955). The method is in women_labor.py and docs/analysis/women-labor-2026-10/README.md.
labor_sex.women_labor.how_to_read: In 2020-2024 the 15 municipios of the Eastern Region had 183,952 women 16 and over (± 1,752), and 42.0% (± 0.8 points) of them were in the labor force, against 41.9% for the rest of the island: a difference of 0.1 points with a margin of ± 0.9, so not significant. Adjusted to the age mix of the rest of the island, the region's rate is 40.7%: the region's women are slightly younger, which raises its unadjusted rate by 1.3 points, while lower participation at 55 and over lowers it by 1.2 points in total. The plain average of the 15 municipio rates, 42.6%, gives Culebra the same weight as Humacao; the pooled rate is the region's own. From 2010-2014 to 2020-2024 the region's women's rate rose 1.3 points (± 1.1), a significant change, and its rate for women 25 to 54 rose 7.8 points (± 1.9).
caveats: A survey estimate, not a count: every value has a 90% margin of error (the Analysis tab shows it); two areas differ significantly only when the difference is larger than its own margin.
Small municipios have wide margins: in 2020-2024 Culebra's women's rate is 64.0% ± 10.4 points and Vieques's 38.6% ± 10.3, so neither can be ranked against most others.

The three windows share no year, so they can be compared with each other; do not set them beside the ACS 5-year windows that overlap them (2016-2020 to 2019-2023, for example), which share years with them.
The margin of a sum of municipios treats their estimates as independent, as the Census Bureau's approximation does; it is an approximation.
The survey's sample (the people and homes it interviewed) is published for 2020-2024 only: in the Eastern Region, 16,930 people and 10,139 housing units.
labor_sex.women_labor.geography: Puerto Rico, the 78 municipalities, and any group of them (the Eastern Region of the ERSV and the seven tourism regions are listed)

methods.nightlights.plain: How bright each barrio and municipio is at night, every month since 2012, from NASA's Black Marble satellite product. Light follows activity and electric power, so it can show growth, decline and blackouts after storms, but it does not count people or homes.
methods.nightlights.plain_es: Cuán brillante es cada barrio y cada municipio de noche, cada mes desde 2012, según el producto satelital Black Marble de la NASA. La luz sigue la actividad y la electricidad, así que puede mostrar crecimiento, declive y apagones después de tormentas, pero no cuenta personas ni hogares.
methods.nightlights.definition: Mean radiance (nW/cm²/sr) of the VNP46A3 pixels whose centre falls in the area, and the share of the area's pixels that the product flags as poor quality (three or fewer clear observations in the month) or gap-filled (none). A municipio's and Puerto Rico's figures pool all their pixels; a year's pools its twelve months.
methods.nightlights.method: nightlights.py lists NASA's LAADS archive of VNP46A3 collection 2 (no login needed), downloads the monthly HDF5 file of tile h11v07 (all of Puerto Rico; h10v07 holds no barrio) with a NASA Earthdata token read from EARTHDATA_TOKEN, and reads the layers AllAngle_Composite_Snow_Free (32-bit radiance, fill value -999.9) and AllAngle_Composite_Snow_Free_Quality (0 good, 1 poor, 2 gap-filled, 255 no value). Each 15 arc-second pixel (about 460 m) counts in the barrio whose outline holds its centre; the three barrios smaller than a pixel take the pixel under them. It keeps a summary per month and deletes the file, and publishes only means and shares, no images. Without the token it stops and changes nothing (docs/nightlights.md).
methods.nightlights.how_to_read: Puerto Rico's mean radiance in 2025 was 5.431 nW/cm²/sr, with 0.2% of its pixels of poor quality or gap-filled. Read the mean radiance together with the quality share: a month with many poor or gap-filled pixels rests on few clear nights.
caveats: Clouds: Puerto Rico is often cloudy, mostly from May to November. A month with few clear nights is flagged poor (three or fewer) or gap-filled (none), and its value can lag the real light.

Moonlight: the product removes moonlight with a model (the lunar BRDF correction), so bright-moon and dark-moon months can be compared; the correction has its own error, largest where the light is dim.
Light is a proxy for activity and for electric power, not a count of people, jobs or homes with power. A change can also come from new LED streetlights, whose whiter light the sensor sees less of.
Pixels are about 460 m across and light spills over borders, so a small or dark barrio next to a bright one reads brighter than it is.
methods.nightlights.source_detail: VNP46A3 collection 2, https://doi.org/10.5067/VIIRS/VNP46A3.002 (LAADS DAAC); Black Marble User Guide v2.0 (October 2024), tables 11 and 12; Román et al. (2018), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2018.03.017. Barrio outlines: barrios.geojson.

layers.oz_tracts.plain: A map layer of the census tracts of Puerto Rico that are Opportunity Zones from 2027 to 2036: purple for zones that are not rural, orange for zones made entirely of rural area, where investors get larger tax benefits.
layers.oz_tracts.plain_es: Una capa del mapa con los sectores censales de Puerto Rico que son Zonas de Oportunidad de 2027 a 2036: morado para las zonas que no son rurales y anaranjado para las zonas formadas por completo por área rural, donde los inversionistas reciben beneficios contributivos mayores.
layers.oz_tracts.definition: oz_tracts.geojson: one polygon per designated tract (178) with g (GEOID), c (2 rural, 1 not rural), m (municipio), t (tract number), p (2020 Census residents), pv (poverty rate, %), mr (median family income as a percent of the area's), b (up to three barrios with the most residents in the tract) and nb (how many barrios have residents in it). Its notes give the counts, the limit and the dates.
layers.oz_tracts.method: opportunity_zones.py takes the designated tracts and their rural status from Treasury's file and the outlines from the Census Bureau's 1:500,000 cartographic file (site/data/geo/tracts.geojson), rounded to 4 decimals. The 2D map (js/facilities.js) and the 3D view (js/facilities3d.js) draw it from the shared list core/facilities.js, filled by rural status, with a legend and a pop-up; the eligible tracts that were not designated are on the Opportunity Zones page, not on this layer.
layers.oz_tracts.how_to_read: A coloured tract is a zone from January 1, 2027: orange if rural, purple if not. Click it for its municipio, barrios, residents and the poverty rate and income Treasury used. An uncoloured tract is not a zone of the second round; the first round's zones, which covered nearly all of Puerto Rico, end on December 31, 2027.
caveats: The outlines are generalised (1:500,000): for drawing, not for deciding whether an address is in a zone; use the Census Bureau's geocoder and the official list for that.
A zone is a tax incentive for private investment, not a grant.
layers.oz_tracts.geography: The 178 designated census tracts, in all 78 municipios
layers.oz_tracts.source_detail: US Treasury, 2027 Qualified Opportunity Zone designations (Data Transparency, 2026-10-30; CDFI Fund list of 2026-11-05); US Census Bureau, cartographic boundary file of 2020 census tracts (cb_2020_72_tract_500k).

economy.opportunity_zones.plain: Which of Puerto Rico's census tracts are Opportunity Zones from 2027 to 2036, whether each zone is rural, which tracts were eligible but not chosen, and how many people live in zones in each barrio and municipio. It also gives the first round of zones, which ends in 2027.
economy.opportunity_zones.plain_es: Qué sectores censales de Puerto Rico son Zonas de Oportunidad de 2027 a 2036, si cada zona es rural, qué sectores eran elegibles pero no se escogieron y cuántas personas viven en zonas en cada barrio y municipio. También da la primera ronda de zonas, que termina en 2027.
economy.opportunity_zones.definition: opportunity_zones.json: tracts lists the 981 census tracts of 2020 (columns in tract_fields): id (GEOID), mun (municipio), tract (its number), status (2 a zone made entirely of rural area, 1 a zone that is not rural, 0 eligible as a low-income community but not designated, -1 not eligible), rural (Treasury's rural flag), pov (poverty rate, %), mfi (median family income, $), mfi_pct (median family income as a percent of the comparison area's), area (an index of areas: the metropolitan or micropolitan area, or Puerto Rico outside one, with its median family income), pop and hu (2020 Census residents and housing units), km2 (land) and barrios (the barrios with residents in the tract, most first). barrios (barrio_fields): pop, pop_designated (residents in zones), pop_eligible (residents in eligible tracts, zones included). municipios (muni_fields): tracts, tracts with residents, eligible, designated, rural, residents, residents in zones and in eligible tracts, housing units in zones, land and land in zones. pr holds Puerto Rico's totals, the 25 percent limit and whether it was reached; groups the medians of poverty and income by status; first_round the 2018 zones (863 tracts of 2010: 837 low-income communities, 26 contiguous) and the 2010 Census residents in them.
economy.opportunity_zones.method: opportunity_zones.py reads Treasury's 2027 designations and eligible tracts from its Data Transparency page, checks Puerto Rico's designated tracts against the CDFI Fund's full list (same 178 tracts, same rural status), against eligibility (every one eligible) and against the limit (a quarter of the 712 eligible tracts, rounded up: 178). Residents come from the observatory's crosswalk (2020 Census blocks counted whole in their tract and, by internal point, in their barrio), so tracts, barrios and municipios add up exactly. The law's test (median family income at most 70% of the area's, or poverty 20% or more with income at most 125%) applied to Treasury's figures gives exactly Treasury's list of eligible tracts. The first round is the CDFI Fund's 2018 list with the 2010 Census residents of TIGERweb.
economy.opportunity_zones.how_to_read: 178 tracts are zones: 96 not rural and 82 rural, with 676,727 residents (20.6% of Puerto Rico in the 2020 Census); every municipio has at least one. 712 tracts were eligible. In the first round, 863 tracts were zones, with 97.5% of the 2010 Census residents.
caveats: A zone is a federal tax incentive for private investment, not a grant: the file says where it applies, not whether anyone invested.
Poverty and income are survey estimates (ACS 2020-2024) with margins of error, as Treasury published them; Treasury's file is the official list.
The two rounds use different census tracts (2010 and 2020): compare their counts and shares, not tract by tract.
economy.opportunity_zones.geography: The 981 census tracts of 2020, the 901 barrios with residents and the 78 municipios; Puerto Rico's totals
economy.opportunity_zones.source_detail: US Treasury, Office of Tax Policy, Data Transparency for Qualified Opportunity Zones: OZ2-Designations-2027-Data-Transparency-10302026.xlsx and OZ2-Eligible-Tracts-Data-Transparency-10302026.xlsx (https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/tax-policy/data-transparency/qualified-opportunity-zones); CDFI Fund, full list of designated QOZs (2026-11-05) and designated QOZs of 2018 (https://www.cdfifund.gov/opportunity-zones); US Census Bureau, 2020 Census blocks and TIGERweb Census 2010 tracts.

population.acs_child_poverty_pct.plain: Out of every 100 children under 18, how many live in a family whose income is below the poverty level.
population.acs_child_poverty_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 menores de 18 años, cuántos viven en una familia con ingreso bajo el nivel de pobreza.
population.acs_child_poverty_pct.definition: The children under 18 whose income in the past 12 months was below the federal poverty level, divided by the children under 18 for whom the survey determines poverty status (table B17001), in percent. A child has the poverty status of the family they live in.
population.acs_child_poverty_pct.method: The observatory reads table B17001 (Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows. It adds the twelve cells of boys and girls under 18 below the poverty level (004-009 and 018-023) and the twelve at or above it (033-038 and 047-052), and divides the first sum by the two together. The poverty level is the federal one, the same in Puerto Rico as in the states. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
population.acs_child_poverty_pct.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 54.9% of the children under 18 of Puerto Rico were below the poverty level (margin ±0.51), against 56.3% in 2017-2021. The share is lowest in Dorado (33.1%), Culebra (33.5%) and Guaynabo (33.6%); it is highest in Vieques (87.5%), Adjuntas (76.6%) and Las Marías (76.2%). The margin of error is above 30% of the estimate for 1 of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024.
caveats: Published for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico only: below the municipality the share is flagged less reliable for 69% of the barrios and 65% of the census tracts (2020-2024) (docs/small-area.md). The poverty rate of all ages (housing.poverty_pct) is published for barrios and census tracts.
Small municipalities have wide margins: read Culebra and Vieques with theirs.
Adjacent five-year windows share four of their five years, so a change from one window to the next is not a trend to read closely.
population.acs_child_poverty_pct.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B17001 (Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age), table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ (vintages 2021 to 2024). The cells used are checked against the Census Bureau's own labels, https://api.census.gov/data/{vintage}/acs/acs5/groups/B17001.json, in every vintage at every build.

population.acs_pan_hh_pct.plain: Out of every 100 households, how many received nutrition assistance (PAN) in the past 12 months.
population.acs_pan_hh_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 hogares, cuántos recibieron asistencia nutricional (PAN) en los últimos 12 meses.
population.acs_pan_hh_pct.definition: Households in which someone received benefits of the Programa de Asistencia Nutricional (PAN) in the past 12 months, divided by all households (table B22010, cell 002 over cell 001), in percent. The Census Bureau's table is titled Food Stamps/SNAP; the Puerto Rico questionnaire asks about the Nutritional Assistance Program and tells people not to count WIC, school lunches or food banks.
population.acs_pan_hh_pct.method: The observatory reads table B22010 (Receipt of Food Stamps/SNAP in the Past 12 Months by Disability Status for Households) of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year files, for each of the four five-year windows, and divides the households that received the benefit (002) by all households (001). The same arithmetic makes the value for a municipality, a barrio, a census tract; block groups are not published by the observatory. The margin of error follows the Census Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of its cells, and a share uses the Bureau's proportion formula. A cell the Census Bureau leaves empty gives no value, never a zero. A share whose margin works out to zero (a share of exactly 100%, for example) is published without a margin. The Puerto Rico value is the Census Bureau's own island row. The code is small_area.py in the project's repository.
population.acs_pan_hh_pct.how_to_read: In 2020-2024, 47.4% of the households of Puerto Rico received nutrition assistance (margin ±0.33), against 43.8% in 2017-2021. The share is lowest in Guaynabo (25.8%), Trujillo Alto (34.3%) and Carolina (34.5%); it is highest in Lares (67.6%), Ciales (67.3%) and Comerío (66.2%). In 2020-2024 the margin of error is above 30% of the estimate (the map hatches such values and the CSV by area marks them as less reliable) for 0% of municipalities, 34% of barrios and 20% of census tracts that have a value.
caveats: It is what households told the survey, not the program's records: surveys usually count fewer recipients than a program's own files. The Administración de Desarrollo Socioeconómico de la Familia (ADSEF) runs the program and holds the official counts; the observatory does not have them by municipio.
It counts households, not people, and not the amount received.
Below the municipality the figure is a rough survey estimate: read it with its margin of error and see methods.small_area_estimates for how large the margins are.
Adjacent five-year windows share four of their five years, so a change from one window to the next is not a trend to read closely.
population.acs_pan_hh_pct.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; also 901 barrios and 981 census tracts (not published for block groups)
population.acs_pan_hh_pct.source_detail: ACS 5-year table B22010 (Receipt of Food Stamps/SNAP in the Past 12 Months by Disability Status for Households), table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/ (vintages 2021 to 2024). The cells used are checked against the Census Bureau's own labels, https://api.census.gov/data/{vintage}/acs/acs5/groups/B22010.json, in every vintage at every build. The question is number 15 of the housing section of the Puerto Rico Community Survey questionnaire, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/methodology/questionnaires/2023/quest23PR.pdf.

econ_inflation.inflation.plain: The data behind the Inflation page: Puerto Rico's official consumer price index (DTRH) and the US CPI-U (BLS) by month since 2000, their 12-month inflation rates, the average of each year, the 8 major groups, a projection to five years ahead with 80% and 95% bands, the test of five forecasting methods, median household income in current and constant dollars, and Social Security's cost-of-living adjustments.
econ_inflation.inflation.definition: inflation.json holds: latest (the newest month of each source); headline (the latest 12-month rates of Puerto Rico and the US for the same month, the rise of prices since January 2000, December 2006 and January 2020, and the average yearly rate since December 2006); monthly (from start, January 2000: pr_yoy and us_yoy, the 12-month change of each index in percent, null when a month is missing, and pr_index and us_index, the index values; Puerto Rico's base is December 2006 = 100, the US base 1982-84 = 100); annual (the change of the yearly average index over the year before); projection (origin, the month each path starts after; end; expected, the Cleveland Fed's expected US inflation over 1 to 10 years; forwards, the expected rate of each single year ahead; spf, the Survey of Professional Forecasters' latest median CPI forecasts; pr_path and us_path, rows of [month, central, lo80, hi80, lo95, hi95] of the 12-month rate; pr_years and us_years, the same for calendar-year averages, with the months already observed; rmse_year, the method's error over each year ahead); backtest (rmse and bias of five methods at 1 to 5 years, the origins and their count); ardl (the fitted model of Puerto Rico's monthly change: months used, long-run pass-through, constant in points a year); groups (each of the 8 major groups: its weight in DTRH's 2000-01 basket, the 12-month change and the change since January 2020 in Puerto Rico and the US, and Puerto Rico's monthly index from January 2007); power (what $100 of January 2000, December 2006 and January 2020 costs at the latest month, and what $100 of today is projected to cost at the end, with Puerto Rico's 80% range); income (median household income, ACS 1-year, with margins at 90%, in current dollars and in the dollars of ref_year by each place's own index); cola (Social Security's adjustment effective each December, computed from the CPI-W, and a benefit of $1,000 in January 2007 followed to the latest month in current dollars and at Puerto Rico's and US prices); checks (the cross-checks of the sources); sources.
econ_inflation.inflation.method: inflation.py reads DTRH's 'Serie Histórica' workbook (2007 on, all items and the 8 groups) and DTRH's CSV on indicadores.pr (1999 to 2006, and the basket weights), checks the two against each other in every shared month, and reads the BLS CPI-U, CPI-W and the CPI-U major groups from the public API (not seasonally adjusted). A month BLS did not publish (October 2025) is left empty in the rates and read by the model as the geometric mean of its neighbours. The projection carries each index forward from its latest month at the Cleveland Fed's expected US inflation, turned into the rate of each single year, plus the index's own seasonal pattern of the last ten years; the bands are the central path plus or minus 1.28 (80%) and 1.96 (95%) times the method's root mean square error in a backtest over 44 quarterly origins from 2011 to 2021 for Puerto Rico and 88 from 2000 to 2021 for the US, at each horizon. The backtest compares, at 1 to 5 years, the US expectation, an ARDL of Puerto Rico's monthly change on its last month, US inflation this and last month and month dummies (from 2008), the last 12 months, Puerto Rico's own average since 2008, and the US expectation plus the last ten years' gap; each method sees only data up to its origin. Income in constant dollars divides by each place's yearly average index. The cost-of-living adjustments follow Social Security's rule (the July to September CPI-W average over that of the last year with an adjustment, rounded to 0.1%) and match the announced adjustments of 2007 to 2025. The plan is docs/inflation-plan-2026-11.md.
econ_inflation.inflation.how_to_read: In September 2026 Puerto Rico's prices were 3.8% higher than a year before and US prices 3.7%. From January 2000 to September 2026 prices rose 74.9% in Puerto Rico and 99.6% in the US. The projection's central path is about 2.8% a year for both from 2027 to 2031; the 80% band of the next year is about ±2.6 points, because forecasts of yearly inflation have missed by about 2 points on average since 2011, mostly in 2021 and 2022.
caveats: The two indexes are measured differently: DTRH averages prices within items with a geometric mean (since 2010), weights its basket from a 2000-01 survey and gives rent and owners' rent-equivalent much less weight than BLS; part of the long-run gap is measurement.
Puerto Rico's index before 2007 is DTRH's earlier method joined to the current base.
An index measures the change of prices over time, not their level: it cannot say whether Puerto Rico is cheaper or dearer than the United States.
The bands come from a short history and assume the future misses like the past.
Median household income is a survey estimate with a margin of error.

economy.commute_45plus_pct.plain: Out of every 100 workers who travel to a workplace, how many usually need 45 minutes or more to get there. People who work from home are not counted. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 18.7% in 2020-2024.
economy.commute_45plus_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas trabajadoras que viajan a un lugar de trabajo, cuántas suelen tardar 45 minutos o más en llegar. No se cuentan las personas que trabajan desde la casa. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 18.7% en 2020-2024.
economy.commute_45plus_pct.definition: Workers 16 and over who did not work from home and whose usual trip to work takes 45 minutes or more, divided by all such workers, times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B08303. The top is cells 11 to 13 (45 to 59, 60 to 89 and 90 or more minutes). The bottom is cell 1, all workers who did not work from home.
economy.commute_45plus_pct.method: The observatory reads table B08303 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 11, 12 and 13 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.commute_45plus_pct.how_to_read: A value of 19 means that 19 of every 100 workers who travel to work spend 45 minutes or more getting there. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it fell island-wide from 21.8% in 2006-2010 to 18.7% in 2020-2024. The Analysis tab's view 'Job centres and commuting' shades it next to jobs per employed resident. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B08303 (Travel Time to Work), cells 11 to 13 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The base differs from the means-of-transportation shares: it leaves out people who worked from home. The two kinds of shares are not directly comparable.

The base is the Census table's workers 16 and over who did not work from home (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 1,050,989 for Puerto Rico in 2020-2024): the means-of-transportation total minus those who worked from home. It is not the same count as the civilian employed residents in the class-of-worker table (1,150,831 in the same window). Do not multiply this share by 'Employed residents 16+ (ACS)'.

It is the usual travel time reported by the worker. It does not give distance, mode or the workplace. A worker can live in one municipality and work in another; the value belongs to the home municipality.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.8 to ±8.7 points across the 78 municipalities, and 19 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate (18 with an estimate above zero, plus Vieques, which shows 0.0% (± 1.8 points), a sample result).

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 18.3% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 18.7%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Manatí goes from 31.65% (2007-2011) to 23.58% (2008-2012). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.

Different periods side by side. With Year set to Latest, each layer in the view 'Job centres and commuting' uses its own latest period. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the jobs symbols show the 2025 annual average from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), while the commute-time and jobs-per-employed-resident layers show the 2020-2024 survey window. Check the year chip in the legend.
economy.commute_45plus_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B08303 (Travel Time to Work), cells 001 and 011-013; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

economy.workers_16plus.plain: How many residents aged 16 and over had a job (not counting the armed forces), from the American Community Survey. It counts people where they live and is an estimate for a five-year window. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: about 1.15 million in 2020-2024.
economy.workers_16plus.plain_es: Cuántas personas residentes de 16 años o más tenían empleo (sin contar las fuerzas armadas), según la Encuesta sobre la Comunidad (ACS). Cuenta a las personas donde viven y es un estimado para un periodo de cinco años. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: cerca de 1.15 millones en 2020-2024.
economy.workers_16plus.definition: The civilian employed population 16 years and over, both sexes and all classes of worker (American Community Survey, ACS, table B24080, cell 1). A person is employed if, in the week before answering the survey (the Census Bureau's reference week), they did any work as a paid employee or in their own business, worked 15 hours or more without pay in a family business, or had a job and were temporarily away. Members of the armed forces are not in the table. It is the base of the class-of-worker shares: government, self-employed and nonprofit.
economy.workers_16plus.method: The observatory reads table B24080 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. The value and its margin of error are the Census Bureau's published ones (cell 1). The observatory also divides the jobs counted by the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) in a year by this count for the five-year window ending that year to get 'jobs per employed resident' (from 2014, the first QCEW year), so the ratio mixes a one-year numerator with a five-year denominator.
economy.workers_16plus.how_to_read: It counts people, not jobs: someone with two jobs counts once. It counts where people live, so a resident who works in another municipality counts at home. As a count it mostly shows the size of a place. On the Analysis tab a shaded layer shows it per 1,000 residents by default. That divides by the total population of all ages for the window's last year, not by residents 16 and over, so it is not an employment rate. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in people, like the estimate, for example ±1,965. To cite the source number, give the table, the window and the place, for example: 'US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B24080 (Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over), Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' If you took the number from the observatory, also cite Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory.
caveats: It is a five-year average, not a single year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2006-2010 window gives 1,149,431 employed residents for Puerto Rico, 8% more than the observatory's BLS-based employed count for 2010 (labor force minus unemployed, 1,060,969). For 2024 the two are close: 1,150,831 here and 1,152,370 from the BLS-based count. Do not mix the two series in one comparison. For individual municipalities the 2020-2024 survey count runs from 0.66 times (Culebra) to 1.23 times (Utuado) the BLS-based employed count for 2024, so do not use one series for a place and the other for the island.
It is not the number of jobs located in the municipality. For jobs by workplace, see the QCEW series.
Margins grow with the size of the place. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin for 2020-2024 runs from ±135 (Culebra, 710 workers) to ±1,965 (San Juan, 133,578 workers).
The island value is the Census Bureau's own island-wide count, not an average. In the 2026-10 snapshot it equals the sum of the 78 municipal counts in every window.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022.
economy.workers_16plus.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B24080 (Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over), cell 001; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

economy.gov_worker_pct.plain: Out of every 100 employed residents aged 16 and over, how many work for a local, Commonwealth or federal government. It counts where people live, not where the government office is. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 18.4% in 2020-2024.
economy.gov_worker_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas residentes de 16 años o más con empleo, cuántas trabajan para el gobierno municipal, el gobierno central o el gobierno federal. Cuenta donde viven las personas, no donde está la oficina del gobierno. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 18.4% en 2020-2024.
economy.gov_worker_pct.definition: Government workers divided by all employed civilian residents 16 and over, times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B24080. The top adds local government workers (cells 7 and 17), state government workers (cells 8 and 18; in Puerto Rico, the Commonwealth government) and federal government workers (cells 9 and 19); cells 7 to 9 are for males and cells 17 to 19 for females. The bottom is cell 1, all employed civilians 16 and over.
economy.gov_worker_pct.method: The observatory reads table B24080 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 7, 8, 9, 17, 18 and 19 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.gov_worker_pct.how_to_read: A value of 18 means that 18 of every 100 employed residents worked for a government. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it fell island-wide from 25.1% in 2006-2010 to 18.4% in 2020-2024. The Analysis tab does not split local, Commonwealth and federal workers. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B24080 (Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over), cells 7, 8, 9, 17, 18 and 19 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: It counts residents by where they live, not jobs by where they are. A municipality can host many government jobs and still have a modest share of resident government workers, because workers commute. For government jobs by workplace, see the 'Government share of jobs' series, from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW).
Government workers are not a share of all adults. The base is employed residents only.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.9 to ±11.0 points across the 78 municipalities, and 4 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 19.3% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 18.4%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Vieques goes from 32.59% (2015-2019) to 51.97% (2016-2020). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
economy.gov_worker_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B24080 (Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over), cells 001, 007-009 and 017-019; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

economy.nonprofit_worker_pct.plain: Out of every 100 employed residents aged 16 and over, how many work for a nonprofit group. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 3.5% in 2020-2024. The share is small, so the value for a single municipality is rough.
economy.nonprofit_worker_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas residentes de 16 años o más con empleo, cuántas trabajan para una organización sin fines de lucro. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 3.5% en 2020-2024. La proporción es pequeña, así que el valor de un solo municipio es aproximado.
economy.nonprofit_worker_pct.definition: Private not-for-profit wage and salary workers divided by all employed civilian residents 16 and over, times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B24080. The top adds cell 6 (males) and cell 16 (females). The bottom is cell 1, all employed civilians 16 and over. These are employees of organizations that are not run for profit, such as charities, religious groups, and private nonprofit schools and hospitals.
economy.nonprofit_worker_pct.method: The observatory reads table B24080 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 6 and 16 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.nonprofit_worker_pct.how_to_read: A value of 3 means that 3 of every 100 employed residents worked for a nonprofit. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it fell island-wide from 4.1% in 2006-2010 to 3.5% in 2020-2024. Use it for the island or for large municipalities. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B24080 (Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over), cells 6 and 16 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: Small shares make the estimates imprecise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 66 of the 78 municipalities have a margin of error larger than 30% of the estimate for 2020-2024. Do not rank small municipalities on this value.

San Lorenzo has an unexplained jump. In the 2026-10 snapshot, its share is 2.1% in 2006-2010, 24.6% (margin about ± 3.5 points) in 2013-2017, 20.8% in 2016-2020 and 1.4% in 2020-2024. The data do not explain the rise and fall. Do not rely on San Lorenzo's values for the windows from 2011-2015 to 2017-2021 without comparing them with the Census Bureau's table B24080.
It counts the employer's type, not the kind of work. A nurse at a nonprofit hospital counts here; a nurse at a government hospital counts under government workers.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 2.8% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 3.5%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Lorenzo goes from 20.84% (2016-2020) to 9.15% (2017-2021). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
economy.nonprofit_worker_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B24080 (Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over), cells 001, 006 and 016; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

economy.self_employed_pct.plain: Out of every 100 employed residents aged 16 and over, how many run their own business or work for themselves. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 14.8% in 2020-2024.
economy.self_employed_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas residentes de 16 años o más con empleo, cuántas tienen su propio negocio o trabajan por cuenta propia. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 14.8% en 2020-2024.
economy.self_employed_pct.definition: Self-employed workers divided by all employed civilian residents 16 and over, times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B24080. The top adds workers in their own incorporated business (cells 5 for males and 15 for females) and in their own business that is not incorporated (cells 10 and 20). The bottom is cell 1, all employed civilians 16 and over. The Census Bureau's table lists owners of an incorporated business under private for-profit wage and salary workers; the observatory counts them here as self-employed.
economy.self_employed_pct.method: The observatory reads table B24080 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It adds cells 5, 10, 15 and 20 and divides by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.self_employed_pct.how_to_read: A value of 15 means that 15 of every 100 employed residents worked for themselves. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it rose island-wide from 11.8% in 2006-2010 to 14.8% in 2020-2024. The jobs data (Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, QCEW) leave out unincorporated self-employed workers (cells 10 and 20), so that part of this share points to work the jobs data miss. Owners of an incorporated business (cells 5 and 15) can be on a payroll that QCEW counts. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B24080 (Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over), cells 5, 10, 15, 20 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The survey records whether the business is incorporated, not whether it is registered or licensed, so this share mixes formal and informal work. It is a rough indicator of self-employment, not a measure of the informal economy.
Unpaid family workers (cells 11 and 21) and employees of private companies (cells 4 and 14) are not in this share.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.9 to ±13.1 points across the 78 municipalities, and 20 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 14.0% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 14.8%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Vieques goes from 18.22% (2016-2020) to 32.65% (2017-2021). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
economy.self_employed_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B24080 (Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over), cells 001, 005, 010, 015 and 020; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

economy.commute_drive_alone_pct.plain: Out of every 100 workers aged 16 and over, how many usually drive to work alone in a car, truck or van. The base includes people who work from home. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 82.6% in 2020-2024.
economy.commute_drive_alone_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas trabajadoras de 16 años o más, cuántas suelen ir solas al trabajo en carro, camioneta o van. La base incluye a las personas que trabajan desde la casa. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 82.6% en 2020-2024.
economy.commute_drive_alone_pct.definition: Workers 16 and over whose usual means of getting to work is driving alone in a car, truck or van, divided by all workers 16 and over (including people who worked from home), times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B08301. The top is cell 3. The bottom is cell 1. Carpoolers are a separate line (cells 4 to 9) and are not included.
economy.commute_drive_alone_pct.method: The observatory reads table B08301 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 3 by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.commute_drive_alone_pct.how_to_read: A value of 83 means that 83 of every 100 workers usually drove alone to work. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the share rose island-wide from 76.9% in 2006-2010 to 83.4% in 2015-2019 and was 82.6% in 2020-2024. It counts residents by where they live, and says nothing about the distance of the trip. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B08301 (Means of Transportation to Work), cell 3 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The base is all workers 16 and over, including those who worked from home (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 6.1% of Puerto Rico's workers in 2020-2024), so the name says 'workers', not 'commuters'. The value is lower than the share among people who traveled to a workplace.

The base is the Census table's 'workers 16 and over': people who worked at some time in the reference week, according to the Census Bureau's subject definitions (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 1,119,495 for Puerto Rico in 2020-2024). The class-of-worker table counts all civilian employed people, including those with a job who were temporarily away (1,150,831 in the same window). Do not multiply this share by 'Employed residents 16+ (ACS)'.

Driving alone is one of several ways to travel. In the 2026-10 snapshot, driving alone, public transportation, walking and working from home together cover 91.9% of Puerto Rico's workers in 2020-2024; the rest carpool, take a taxi, ride a motorcycle or bicycle, or use other means.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.9 to ±14.2 points across the 78 municipalities, and none is larger than 30% of the estimate.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 86.1% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 82.6%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra goes from 42.96% (2010-2014) to 53.86% (2011-2015). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
economy.commute_drive_alone_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B08301 (Means of Transportation to Work), cells 001 and 003; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

economy.commute_transit_pct.plain: Out of every 100 workers aged 16 and over, how many usually take public transportation to work. The base includes people who work from home. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 0.9% in 2020-2024, down from 3.1% in 2006-2010.
economy.commute_transit_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas trabajadoras de 16 años o más, cuántas suelen usar el transporte colectivo para ir al trabajo. La base incluye a las personas que trabajan desde la casa. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 0.9% en 2020-2024, menos que el 3.1% de 2006-2010.
economy.commute_transit_pct.definition: Workers 16 and over whose usual means of getting to work is public transportation, divided by all workers 16 and over (including people who worked from home), times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B08301. The top is cell 10, 'Public transportation (excluding taxicab)'. It covers bus, subway or elevated rail, train, ferryboat and the carro público line, so riders of carros públicos are counted here. The Census Bureau labels that line 'Light rail, streetcar or trolley (carro público in Puerto Rico)', cell 14, from the window ending 2019, and 'Streetcar or trolley car (carro publico in Puerto Rico)', cell 12, in earlier windows. The bottom is cell 1. Taxicab is a separate line and is not included.
economy.commute_transit_pct.method: The observatory reads table B08301 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 10 by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.commute_transit_pct.how_to_read: A value of 1 means that 1 of every 100 workers usually took public transportation to work. It describes what residents report, not the service available. For service, see the share of residents near a scheduled stop. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B08301 (Means of Transportation to Work), cell 10 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The base is all workers 16 and over, including those who worked from home (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 6.1% of Puerto Rico's workers in 2020-2024), so the name says 'workers', not 'commuters'.

A value of 0.0 is a sample result, not proof that nobody rides. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 25 of the 78 municipalities show 0.0% for 2020-2024. Orocovis has the highest value, 3.7%, with a margin of ± 2.8 points; San Juan has the second highest, 3.4% (± 0.4 points).

The base is the Census table's 'workers 16 and over': people who worked at some time in the reference week, according to the Census Bureau's subject definitions (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 1,119,495 for Puerto Rico in 2020-2024). The class-of-worker table counts all civilian employed people, including those with a job who were temporarily away (1,150,831 in the same window). Do not multiply this share by 'Employed residents 16+ (ACS)'.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.1 to ±3.2 points across the 78 municipalities, and 76 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate (51 with an estimate above zero, plus the 25 that show 0.0%).
In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island share fell from 3.1% to 0.9% between the 2006-2010 and 2020-2024 windows. The data do not say why.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 0.3% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 0.9%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Cataño goes from 3.78% (2017-2021) to 1.16% (2018-2022). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
economy.commute_transit_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B08301 (Means of Transportation to Work), cells 001 and 010; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

economy.commute_walk_pct.plain: Out of every 100 workers aged 16 and over, how many usually walk to work. The base includes people who work from home. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 2.4% in 2020-2024.
economy.commute_walk_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas trabajadoras de 16 años o más, cuántas suelen ir a pie al trabajo. La base incluye a las personas que trabajan desde la casa. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 2.4% en 2020-2024.
economy.commute_walk_pct.definition: Workers 16 and over whose usual means of getting to work is walking, divided by all workers 16 and over (including people who worked from home), times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B08301. The top is cell 19, 'Walked'. The bottom is cell 1.
economy.commute_walk_pct.method: The observatory reads table B08301 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 19 by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.commute_walk_pct.how_to_read: A value of 2 means that 2 of every 100 workers usually walked to work. In the 2026-10 snapshot, it fell island-wide from 3.9% in 2006-2010 to 2.4% in 2020-2024. Bicycle is a separate line and is not included. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B08301 (Means of Transportation to Work), cell 19 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The base is all workers 16 and over, including those who worked from home (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 6.1% of Puerto Rico's workers in 2020-2024), so the name says 'workers', not 'commuters'.

The shares are small, so most municipal values are imprecise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Patillas has the highest value for 2020-2024, 10.8%, with a margin of ± 4.6 points, and Arroyo shows 0.0% (± 0.5 points), a sample result and not proof that nobody walks.

The base is the Census table's 'workers 16 and over': people who worked at some time in the reference week, according to the Census Bureau's subject definitions (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 1,119,495 for Puerto Rico in 2020-2024). The class-of-worker table counts all civilian employed people, including those with a job who were temporarily away (1,150,831 in the same window). Do not multiply this share by 'Employed residents 16+ (ACS)'.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.2 to ±6.5 points across the 78 municipalities, and 74 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate (73 with an estimate above zero, plus Arroyo at 0.0%).

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 2.2% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 2.4%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Culebra goes from 24.66% (2011-2015) to 16.33% (2012-2016). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
economy.commute_walk_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B08301 (Means of Transportation to Work), cells 001 and 019; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).

economy.work_from_home_pct.plain: Out of every 100 workers aged 16 and over, how many worked from home. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico: 6.1% in 2020-2024, up from 2.2% in 2006-2010.
economy.work_from_home_pct.plain_es: De cada 100 personas trabajadoras de 16 años o más, cuántas trabajaron desde la casa. En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Puerto Rico: 6.1% en 2020-2024, más que el 2.2% de 2006-2010.
economy.work_from_home_pct.definition: Workers 16 and over who worked from home, divided by all workers 16 and over, times 100. Source: American Community Survey (ACS) table B08301. The top is cell 21 (labeled 'Worked from home' from the window ending 2019 and 'Worked at home' in earlier windows). The bottom is cell 1.
economy.work_from_home_pct.method: The observatory reads table B08301 for every five-year window from the Census Bureau's summary files: per-sequence files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and table-based files for windows ending 2021 and later. It keeps the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. It divides cell 21 by cell 1. The margin of error is calculated by the observatory from the published margins of the cells used: margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares, and the share's margin uses the Census Bureau's formula for a proportion whose numerator is part of its denominator. If that formula would need the square root of a negative number, the observatory uses the Census Bureau's ratio formula instead. Shares are kept to two decimals; the Analysis tab shows one.
economy.work_from_home_pct.how_to_read: A value of 6 means that 6 of every 100 workers worked from home. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island share stays between 2.15% and 2.34% in every window from 2006-2010 to 2015-2019, then rises: 3.1% in 2016-2020 and 6.1% in 2020-2024. A five-year window blends earlier and later years, so while the share is rising it lags behind the latest level. The number after the plus-minus sign (±) is the margin of error: with 90% confidence, the true value lies within that distance of the estimate. The Analysis tab prints it in percentage points, for example ±0.4 pts. The percentage is not printed in the Census Bureau's table; the observatory calculates it from the cells named in the definition. To cite it: 'Share calculated by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, from US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B08301 (Means of Transportation to Work), cell 21 divided by cell 1, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico.' To cite the Census Bureau's own numbers, cite the table cells, not the percentage.
caveats: The shares are small in most municipalities, so values are imprecise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Vieques has the highest value for 2020-2024, 24.0%, with a margin of ± 10.9 points, and three municipalities (Jayuya, Maunabo and Yabucoa) show 0.0%, a sample result and not proof that nobody works from home.

Small municipalities are less precise. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the margin of error for 2020-2024 runs from ±0.1 to ±10.9 points across the 78 municipalities, and 59 of the 78 are larger than 30% of the estimate (56 with an estimate above zero, plus the 3 that show 0.0%).

The base is the Census table's 'workers 16 and over': people who worked at some time in the reference week, according to the Census Bureau's subject definitions (in the 2026-10 snapshot, 1,119,495 for Puerto Rico in 2020-2024). The class-of-worker table counts all civilian employed people, including those with a job who were temporarily away (1,150,831 in the same window). Do not multiply this share by 'Employed residents 16+ (ACS)'.
Workers who worked from home are also in the base of the other means-of-transportation shares (drive alone, public transportation, walk), but not in the base of the commute-time share.

The Puerto Rico share is calculated from the Census Bureau's island-wide counts, not averaged from the 78 municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the middle (median) municipality has 4.4% for 2020-2024 and the island value is 6.1%.

Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2012, 2017 and 2022. In some municipalities one new year can move the value a lot. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Vieques goes from 6.53% (2015-2019) to 17.54% (2016-2020). Do not read a trend from one small municipality.
economy.work_from_home_pct.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, table B08301 (Means of Transportation to Work), cells 001 and 021; windows from 2006-2010 to the latest published (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
